# Migration guide template

Use this template when documenting breaking changes in **Boilerplate templates**. Boilerplate leverages Copier's automated template update mechanism to handle migrations. Migration guides focus on what the automation does, edge cases requiring manual intervention, and validation procedures.

Important

This template is for **template migrations** (projects updating to new template versions via `copier update`). CLI breaking changes have no migration guide — they're communicated through the changelog's **BREAKING** entry and the release notes; see [Versioning & Compatibility Policy § Two Breaking-Change Paths](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/governance/versioning/#two-breaking-change-paths).

**Reference**: [Versioning and migration](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/versioning/index.md)

______________________________________________________________________

## Template

````markdown
# Migration guide: <feature or tool> v<OLD_VERSION> → v<NEW_VERSION>

## What's changing

[1–2 sentence summary of the breaking change and why it was necessary.]

### Example

Before (v<OLD_VERSION>):
```python
# Old way
from boilerplate import render_template
result = render_template("my-template", answers={...})
````

After (v\<NEW_VERSION>):

```python
# New way
from boilerplate import Composer
result = Composer("my-template", answers={...}).render()
```

## Automated migration

Copier handles this migration automatically when you update your project:

```powershell
# Update to latest template version
copier update
```

### What the automation does

The update process will:

1. **Update configuration**: Automatically transform `<old_config>` to `<new_config>` format.
1. **Rename files**: Move `old_structure/` to `new_structure/` preserving your customizations.
1. **Update imports**: Replace deprecated import paths with new ones in `.py` files.
1. **Merge conflicts**: Leave conflict markers in files where your customizations and the template change overlap.

**No manual intervention needed** for these transformations.

### Files affected

| File pattern            | Change                      | Automatic | Manual review needed       |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------- | --------- | -------------------------- |
| `pyproject.toml`        | Version pins updated        | ✓         | No                         |
| `src/**/*.py`           | Import paths updated        | ✓         | Verify custom imports      |
| `.vscode/settings.json` | New settings added          | ✓         | Merge with custom settings |
| `README.md`             | Template sections refreshed | ✓         | Preserve custom content    |

## Manual intervention (if needed)

### Scenario 1: Custom <component> modifications

**If** you have heavily customized `<component>`, the automated merge may require review:

```powershell
# After running update, check for merge markers
git diff
```

Look for conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`). Resolve by choosing the appropriate sections or merging both.

### Scenario 2: External dependencies on old API

**If** you have external scripts or tools calling the old API:

```python
# Update external scripts from:
old_function(param1, param2)

# To:
new_function(param1=param1, param2=param2)
```

These changes are **outside** the template-managed files and require manual updates.

## Testing and validation

Verify the automated migration succeeded:

```powershell
# Run quality gates
uv run ruff check --no-fix
uv run pyright
uv run pytest
```

**Expected results**:

- ✓ No linting errors
- ✓ No type checking errors
- ✓ All tests pass
- ✓ Application starts successfully: `uv run python -m <your_app>`

## Rollback procedure

If critical issues arise:

```powershell
# Option 1: Revert the update commit
git revert HEAD
uv sync --locked

# Option 2: Restore from backup (if you created one)
git checkout <branch-before-update>
```

Then open an issue with:

- The error encountered
- Your project structure (especially customizations)
- Output from `boilerplate --version` or `copier --version`

## Troubleshooting

### Merge conflicts during automated update

**Symptom**: Copier leaves conflict markers and exits 0.

**Cause**: Your customizations conflict with template changes.

**Solution**:

```bash
# Review conflicts
git status
# Edit files with markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>)
# Choose appropriate sections
git add <resolved-files>
git commit -m "chore: resolve migration conflicts"
```

### Type errors after migration

**Symptom**: `pyright` reports type mismatches in updated code.

**Cause**: API signature changes not fully applied to custom code.

**Solution**:

```powershell
# Identify failing imports/calls
uv run python -m pyright --verbose
# Update your custom code to match new signatures (see examples above)
```

### Tests fail after update

**Symptom**: Previously passing tests now fail.

**Cause**: Breaking changes in behavior, not just API.

**Solution**:

```powershell
# Review test failures for deprecated patterns
uv run python -m pytest -v
# Update test assertions and mocks to match new behavior
```

## Getting help

- Review the [<Feature> documentation](link).
- Search existing GitHub issues: [Link to GitHub search]
- Open a new issue with your error and environment details: [Link to new issue template]

## Summary of changes

| Component | What changed       | Why                          |
| --------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| Config    | Property renamed   | Improved clarity             |
| API       | Function signature | Enhanced flexibility         |
| CLI       | Command structure  | Consistency with other tools |

## Timeline

| Version | Status     | Support until   |
| ------- | ---------- | --------------- |
| v1.x    | Deprecated | [ISO-8601 date] |
| v2.0    | Current    | Ongoing         |

______________________________________________________________________

_Migration guide created: [ISO-8601 date]_

_For latest updates, see the [release notes](link)._

````

---

## Checklist: before publishing a migration guide

- Provide clear rationale for the breaking change.
- Include at least one before/after code example.
- Document what the automated migration does (file transformations, renames, updates).
- List all affected file patterns with automatic vs. manual review indicators.
- Identify scenarios requiring manual intervention (customizations, external dependencies).
- Provide validation steps (quality gates, application startup).
- Explain rollback procedure (git revert, restore from backup).
- Provide troubleshooting for common automated migration issues (merge conflicts, type errors).
- Link to detailed documentation for behavior changes.
- Specify deprecation timeline (when old version ends support).
- Test the automated migration on a sample project before publishing.
- Have a Boilerplate maintainer review before merging.

## Where next

Return to [Versioning and migration](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/versioning/index.md) for the policy this template documents, and hand the finished guide off through [Versioning & compatibility](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/governance/versioning/index.md).```
````

# Compose and update with plain Copier

A Boilerplate project is plain Copier output: one `.copier-answers.<layer>.yml` per layer, each written by Copier. You can compose a project and update its layers with `copier` alone. This page shows the commands, what they leave out, and which layers can update.

## Run Copier where Boilerplate is importable

The `project` template loads extensions from the `boilerplate` package and from `copier-template-extensions`, and Copier runs template code only with `--trust`. Run `copier` from a checkout of the repository, which has both:

```bash
BP=/path/to/boilerplate    # your checkout
uv run --project "$BP" copier --version
```

The compose commands below use `uv run --project "$BP" copier` and run from the folder that holds your project, so `--project` leaves the working directory alone; the update command runs from the project root.

## Compose `streamlit` over `project`

Two `copier copy` runs build what `boilerplate new streamlit` builds. Run `project` first, with the two defaults `streamlit` overrides:

```bash
uv run --project "$BP" copier copy --trust --defaults \
  --data project_name="Probe App" \
  --data description="A probe." \
  --data author_name="Ada Probe" \
  --data author_email=ada@example.com \
  --data 'dependencies=["streamlit","pydantic>=2"]' \
  --data sample_module=false \
  "$BP/src/boilerplate/templates/project" probe-app
```

Then remove the project's `README.md` and run `streamlit` over it, reading `project`'s answers and supplying the two values it never records:

```bash
rm probe-app/README.md
uv run --project "$BP" copier copy --trust --defaults --overwrite \
  --data-file probe-app/.copier-answers.project.yml \
  --data project_slug=probe-app \
  --data package_name=probe_app \
  "$BP/src/boilerplate/templates/streamlit" probe-app
```

| Step                                             | Why                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dependencies`, `sample_module` on the first run | `streamlit` overrides both defaults, and `project` renders `pyproject.toml` and the sample module from them.                                                                                                    |
| `rm probe-app/README.md`                         | `streamlit` lists `README.md` in `_skip_if_exists`. Copier honors that list over `--overwrite`; `boilerplate new` ignores it.                                                                                   |
| `project_slug`, `package_name`                   | `project` computes both from `project_name` (`probe-app`, `probe_app`) and never records them. Without `package_name`, Copier silently skips every file in a `<package_name>` folder under `src/` and `tests/`. |

`project`'s post-generation tasks run in the first command, before `streamlit`'s files exist. Add `--skip-tasks` there to run them yourself afterwards.

### What differs from `boilerplate new`

The rendered files are identical. Two things differ:

| File                            | By hand                                                                                          | `boilerplate new`                   |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| `boilerplate.lock`              | Not written.                                                                                     | Written.                            |
| `.copier-answers.streamlit.yml` | Records only `streamlit`'s own questions: `container_registry`, `dependencies`, `sample_module`. | Also records `project`'s questions. |

## Update a git-backed layer

A layer updates with `copier update` when its answers file records a `_commit`, which means its template came from a git repository. From the project root, with the working tree committed (Copier refuses a dirty tree):

```bash
uv run --project "$BP" copier update --trust --defaults \
  --answers-file .copier-answers.streamlit.yml \
  --data-file .copier-answers.project.yml \
  --data project_slug=probe-app \
  --data package_name=probe_app \
  --vcs-ref <tag>
```

Copier accepts `--data-file` once: a second flag stops with `Switch --data-file already given`. Pass the answers file of the layer's direct parent (`project`'s file, since `streamlit` extends `project`). A base layer such as `project` needs none.

- A parent's file that `boilerplate new` wrote also records the parent's own ancestors' answers.
- A file from a by-hand `copier copy`, or one an earlier by-hand update trimmed, holds only that parent's own questions. Supply the rest with `--data key=value`, which wins over the same key in the file.

Pass the two derived names too, as in the compose step: no answers file records them. Without `package_name`, Copier exits 0 and silently skips every file in a `<package_name>` folder under `src/` and `tests/`. Use the names your project has.

Omit `--vcs-ref` to take the latest tag. Update one layer at a time, lower layers first: the `layers` list in `boilerplate.lock` is the order, and without a lock you read the templates' `extends` chains. `_src_path` in each answers file must be an absolute path or URL.

Two limits come with updating one layer by hand:

- **The answers file shrinks.** After the update, the layer's file holds only the questions its own `copier.yml` declares, so answers inherited from a parent drop out of it. The `--data-file` supplies them from then on, so pass it on every update: without it, the next update renders the inherited answers empty.
- **A changed line that renders an unrecorded value conflicts.** Copier renders the old copy from the answers file alone, so a value the file lacks, such as the computed `package_name`, renders empty there and your rendered value reads as your edit. A release that changes that line produces an inline conflict (`<<<<<<<`) in that file and nowhere else. `--data` and `--data-file` do not help, because neither reaches the old copy. Resolve the conflict in the file and commit.

## Bundled layers are copy-only

`boilerplate new` renders `project` and `streamlit` from the template folders inside the installed package. Those folders are not git repository roots, so Copier records no `_commit` in `.copier-answers.project.yml` or `.copier-answers.streamlit.yml`, and `copier update` stops with "cannot obtain old template references". This holds for the by-hand compose above too, which uses the same folders. A layer you render from a git repository updates; to refresh a bundled layer, run its `copier copy` command again.

Back to [Template composition](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/composition/index.md) · Next: [Versioning and migration](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/versioning/index.md)

# Project template

The project template creates a general-purpose Python project, with its tools configured.

## Features

- **Modern toolchain**: uv, Ruff, Pyright, Pytest
- **VS Code integration**: Pinned settings and recommended extensions
- **Type safety**: Full type hint coverage
- **Testing**: Pytest with an example module and matching test
- **Notebooks**: A starter Jupyter notebook

## Project structure

For a project named `my-app` (package `my_app`):

```text
my-app/
├── pyproject.toml          # Metadata + tool config (ruff, pyright, pytest)
├── README.md               # Project documentation
├── .gitignore
├── .gitattributes          # LF line endings on every platform
├── .vscode/                # VS Code settings
│   ├── settings.json
│   └── extensions.json
├── notebooks/
│   └── notebook.ipynb      # Starter notebook
├── src/
│   └── my_app/             # Source code
│       ├── __init__.py     # Package version
│       └── module.py       # Example `add(a, b)` function (sample_module, default on)
├── tests/
│   └── my_app/
│       ├── test_module.py  # Tests for the example module (sample_module, default on)
│       └── test_import.py  # Checks the package imports (sample_module off)
├── uv.lock                 # Pinned deps (written by the post-generation tasks)
├── .copier-answers.project.yml  # This layer's answers, for future updates
└── boilerplate.lock        # Each layer's version, source and checksum
```

`README.md` and `src/<package>/__init__.py` are project-owned: the template lists them in `_skip_if_exists`, which [governs what an update does to them](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/04-composition-engine/#per-layer-render-loop).

Post-generation tasks create the virtual environment and `uv.lock` and initialize a git repository (skipped with `--no-tasks`). With `--no-tasks`, the cleanup step also never runs, so `_scripts/post_generation.py` is left behind in the generated project — it isn't gitignored.

## Usage

```powershell
# Create new project (template name, then destination)
boilerplate new project ./my-app
cd my-app

# Run tests
uv run pytest
```

The post-generation tasks already ran `uv sync`, so the environment is ready. If you passed `--no-tasks`, run `uv sync` before the first `uv run`.

Add dependencies with `uv add <pkg>` (see [Add a dependency](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/environment/#1-start-or-clone-a-project)); `pyproject.toml` holds project metadata, entry points and scripts, and the tool configuration described under [Configuration](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/environment/#configuration).

## The sample module

`module.py` and its test are a starting point, not scaffolding you must keep. Answer `sample_module` with no to render without them: `boilerplate new project ./my-app --data sample_module=false`. `tests/<package>/test_import.py` renders in their place, so `uv run pytest` still has a test to run. A template that extends `project` can set the default to off in its own `copier.yml`.

## Choose a build backend

The build backend turns the project into a wheel and an sdist. The `build_backend` question sets the `[build-system]` table in `pyproject.toml`: `uv_build` by default, `hatchling` when you answer it that way: `boilerplate new project ./my-app --data build_backend=hatchling`.

| Pick                 | Choose it when                                                                                  | Renders                                                                         |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `uv_build` (default) | The code is pure Python with a static version and one `src/<package>`, and uv is your toolchain | `requires = ["uv_build>=0.13,<0.14"]` and nothing else                          |
| `hatchling`          | You need build hooks, plugins, a version from git tags (`hatch-vcs`), or a custom file layout   | `requires = ["hatchling>=1.27"]` and a `[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]` table |

The `uv_build` range names the current uv minor, and the [Streamlit template](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/index.md)'s Dockerfile installs the same minor, so uv runs its bundled backend and fetches nothing from a package index. A newer uv still builds, with a warning on each `uv sync` until you raise the cap. An older uv fetches `uv-build` from your default index, so a private `package_index_url` must mirror it.

`uv_build` builds from static metadata and ships a git-ignored file that sits inside the package directory. If you need a dynamic version or generated files in the package tree, pick `hatchling`.

Compiled code (Rust through maturin, C or C++ through scikit-build-core) is a hand edit: replace the `[build-system]` table, then follow uv's [extension module guide](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/init/#projects-with-extension-modules). The template scaffolds no `Cargo.toml` or `CMakeLists.txt`. [ADR-017](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-017-build-backend/index.md) compares nine backends and holds the reasoning behind these two.

## Where next

Need a Streamlit UI on top of this? See the [Streamlit template](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/index.md). Building your own template? Start with [Template authoring](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/authoring/index.md). Return to the [Templates Hub](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/index.md).

# Versioning and migration

Template versions evolve independently from the CLI. Breaking changes are managed through semantically versioned major bumps paired with automated migration support via Copier's three-way merge system.

## Version format

Templates use semantic versioning (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`), independent from the CLI version:

```yaml
# boilerplate.yml
version: "0.1.0"  # Template version (independent from CLI)
name: project
extends:
  - base@1.0.0  # exact pin
```

`extends` accepts an exact version pin (`name@1.0.0`) or an unversioned reference (`name`); range specifiers such as `^1.0` are not accepted; [Design — Template system § `extends` syntax](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/03-template-system/#extends-syntax) reserves them.

**Key**: Each template versions itself, not tied to Boilerplate CLI versions.

### When to bump

A template version moves once per release, measured from the last released version of that template. Take the smallest step the whole unreleased change set requires (pre-1.0: MINOR for a breaking change, PATCH otherwise) and land it once. A later unreleased change raises that step if it needs a bigger one; it MUST NOT add another bump. Bumping per change or per pull request produces version numbers no consumer ever saw.

## Templates vs. projects

**Templates** (versioned in `boilerplate.yml`): source code with `boilerplate.yml`, `copier.yml`, and template files.

A project generated from a template is not itself versioned; it tracks each composed layer's source, version, and commit in one `.copier-answers.<layer>.yml` per layer. `boilerplate new` also writes `boilerplate.lock`, which records each layer's name, version, source, commit (null for a layer rendered from a plain folder, such as the bundled templates) and template checksum, plus a hash of each answers file. No command reads it yet. The schema is in [Design — Data models § BoilerplateLock](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/02-data-models/#boilerplatelock).

## Migration-first philosophy

Breaking changes in templates are acceptable **IF** automated migration is provided.

### Why automated migration?

- **Preservation**: Projects preserve user customizations during updates
- **Safety**: Three-way merge (old template + user changes + new template) minimizes conflicts
- **Visibility**: Users see what changed and can make informed decisions
- **Scalability**: Enables evolution of templates without cascading manual work

For a worked rename migration, see [Template authoring § Rename through a staged move](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/authoring/#rename-through-a-staged-move). A layer rendered from a git repository updates with Copier's own `copier update`; the layers bundled in the package are [copy-only](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/plain-copier/#bundled-layers-are-copy-only). A project built from more than one layer has no shipped update command yet: each layer must render from the composition's merged schema, which only `boilerplate update` will provide ([ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md) records that design). Run `copier update` on a child layer alone, such as `streamlit`, and it exits 0 while skipping every path under the package directory and dropping the inherited answers from that layer's answers file.

## What constitutes a breaking change

### Breaking changes (require automated migration)

- Removing template variables (Copier questions)
- Renaming template variables
- Changing variable type or validation rules
- Moving or renaming generated files
- Restructuring project directory layout
- Changing template metadata format
- Changing composition constraints (`extends` version requirements)

### Non-breaking changes (minor or patch)

- Adding new template variables (optional, with defaults)
- Adding new files
- Improving templates (content updates)
- Bug fixes to generated files
- Adding new composition methods
- Deprecating template variables (with backward compat handler)

## Semantic versioning for templates

### Pre-1.0 template versioning (0.x)

Templates in early development use `0.x.y` versioning. Semantic versioning rules differ for pre-release versions:

| Bump  | Example       | Semantics                           | Migration                 |
| ----- | ------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| PATCH | 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 | Compatible bug fixes                | None needed               |
| MINOR | 0.1.0 → 0.2.0 | **Breaking changes**                | Copier migration required |
| MAJOR | 0.x.0 → 1.0.0 | Release-ready; begins stable SemVer | Copier migration required |

**Key**: In pre-1.0 versioning, minor bumps signal breaking changes (like major bumps in 1.x+). This reflects that 0.x APIs are unstable and may change frequently.

**Example:**

```yaml
# project template (early development)
version: "0.1.0"  # Initial release
---
version: "0.2.0"  # Minor bump = breaking change (migrate Copier)
---
version: "1.0.0"  # Major bump = stable release (migrate Copier)
---
version: "1.1.0"  # Minor bump = new features (no migration needed)
```

**For template authors**: If your template is pre-1.0, treat minor version bumps like major version bumps—provide Copier migration scripts for any breaking changes.

### PATCH version (bug fixes)

```yaml
# boilerplate.yml (v1.0.1)
version: "1.0.1"  # Patch bump
```

**When to bump PATCH:**

- Fix typo or incorrect content in generated files
- Fix bug in template logic
- Update dependencies without breaking changes

**No migration needed.**

### MINOR version (new features)

```yaml
# boilerplate.yml (v1.1.0)
version: "1.1.0"  # Minor bump
extends:
  - base@1.0.0  # exact pin, unchanged
```

**When to bump MINOR:**

- Add new optional template variables
- Add new template variants
- Extend composition options

**No migration needed** (backward compatible).

### MAJOR version (breaking changes)

```yaml
# boilerplate.yml (v2.0.0)
version: "2.0.0"  # Major bump
extends:
  - base@2.0.0  # exact pin, major bump
```

**When to bump MAJOR:**

- Remove template variables
- Rename template variables
- Restructure project layout
- Change variable types

**Migration is required** via Copier's update mechanism.

## Migration requirements for breaking changes

*`boilerplate update` is design-only ([ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md)): no shipped command of this tool runs migrations. Vanilla `copier update` runs them now for a layer rendered from a git repository, and never for a bundled layer ([copy-only](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/plain-copier/#bundled-layers-are-copy-only)); a child layer of a composed project needs the merged schema that command does not have, so its migrations wait for `boilerplate update`. The bundled layers ship theirs under the rules below; the rules bind template authors either way.*

### Copier migration scripts

Every breaking change ships as one or more entries under `_migrations` in `copier.yml`:

```text
template/
├── boilerplate.yml
├── copier.yml       # _migrations lives here
└── template/
    └── ...project files
```

```yaml
# copier.yml
_migrations:
  - version: "2.0.0"
    when: "{{ _stage == 'before' }}"
    command:
      - "{{ _copier_python }}"
      - -c
      - |
        # move/rename/rewrite logic, guarded by a state check
```

Each entry runs a `command` (a string run through the shell, or a list run directly), optionally gated by `version` (a PEP 440 version: the entry fires only when the update crosses it, from < version \<= to) and `when` (which stage to run in; defaults to the `after` stage), with `working_directory` scoping where the command runs. Typical operations: rename or move a generated file, rewrite import paths or config keys after a rename, create a directory the updated layout needs. See Copier's [migrations documentation](https://copier.readthedocs.io/en/stable/configuring/#migrations) for the full mechanism, and [Template authoring § Rename through a staged move](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/authoring/#rename-through-a-staged-move) for a complete worked entry.

### Authoring rules

A migration is fix-up code, not replayed history: an update may cross several versions at once, and every crossed migration runs against one of two trees — the pre-update tree for `before`-stage entries, the target tree for `after`-stage ones (the default) — never an intermediate one. Four rules follow, specified in [ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/#version-jumps-stay-single-pass-migrations-are-jump-safe-by-authoring-contract):

1. **Jump-safe.** Inspect state before acting and stay idempotent — "if the old path exists, move it," never "the tree is at the previous version, so move it."
1. **Carried forward.** Keep every historical `_migrations` entry in every later release, in ascending version order — Copier reads the list only from the version being updated *to*, and executes it in declaration order rather than sorting by version.
1. **Layer-scoped.** Touch only files your own template owns. Copier has no ownership model; a migration that rewrites a file another layer overrode destroys that override silently.
1. **Conflict-aware.** Migrations run even when the merge left unresolved conflict markers, so a migration that parses a file must tolerate them — and a non-zero exit fails the whole update.

Three further rules govern what an update costs the project. Copier removes every path the new template version stops rendering — by name, without comparing content — and its merge treats a renamed file as added on both sides. The template, not the tool, is where a project's own work survives that. Both behaviours are Copier internals rather than public API, verified against Copier 9.18.1; `tests/boilerplate/templates/test_streamlit_update_migration.py` drives a real update and fails if they change.

1. **Rename through a staged move.** A template that renames or relocates a rendered path MUST ship a `before`-stage migration that moves the project's copy to the new name *and stages the move* (`git mv`, or a move followed by `git add -A -- <old> <new>`). Staging is the load-bearing half: Copier snapshots the index before it merges, so a staged move puts the project's content under the new name on the merge's "before updating" side, and the update pauses on a conflict carrying both versions. Without the migration the project's edited copy is deleted at exit 0 — no conflict marker, no `.rej` file, no message. The worked entry is in [Template authoring](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/authoring/#keeping-a-projects-work).
1. **Render nothing the render's own `.gitignore` matches.** A file git ignores never enters the index, so Copier's merge cannot see it: no three-way merge, no conflict marker, no `.rej` file, and no history to recover it from. A template MUST NOT render a path its own ignore rules match, and MUST NOT ignore a path the render tells the user to commit.
1. **Say who owns each file.** For every rendered file, choose between template-owned — the template keeps changing it, so a project that edits it risks a conflict whenever a release touches the same lines, and on a file small enough that one diff hunk spans it, any release at all ([ADR-015](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-015-idiomatic-artifacts/#verification-2026-07-28)) — and project-owned, listed in `_skip_if_exists` (specified in the [Per-Layer Render Loop](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/04-composition-engine/#per-layer-render-loop)). State the choice where an author will find it; silence means template-owned. A file meant to be deleted (a sample module) stays template-owned; project-owned is for files users are expected to keep and rewrite instead, like a README or an entry point.

### Copier update process

When a project updates, Copier:

1. **Reads** the old template version from that layer's answers file
1. **Refuses to start** unless run with `--trust`, once the update crosses any declared migration — nothing is applied without it
1. **Runs `before`-stage migrations** for every version crossed, against the pre-update tree
1. **Performs three-way merge**:
1. Old template files (v1.x)
1. User changes (what they customized)
1. New template files (v2.0.0)
1. **Runs `after`-stage migrations** — the default stage — for every version crossed, against the merged tree
1. **Leaves conflict markers** in place for incompatibilities

Conflicts do not stop migrations, and Copier's exit code stays 0 through a conflicted update: the conflict pause is where the update model in [ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md) picks up.

## Template organization constraints

### One version stream per repository

**Constraint**: All templates in a Git repository MUST share a single version stream — one tag series versioning the repository as a whole. A template that versions independently MUST therefore resolve to its own repository.

**Rationale**: Copier's version mechanics are repository-wide. It finds "latest" by sorting the repository's Git tags (PEP 440), and it records the project's template version from the nearest tag (`git describe`). Two independently versioned templates sharing a repository would interleave their tags: an update could move one template to the other's release, and a project's answers file could record the wrong template's version. Copier's `_subdirectory` supports multiple templates in one repository only when they release in lockstep under one tag series — and even then at a cost: Copier reads `_subdirectory` from the repository's *root* `copier.yml`, so serving several templates from one repository means a root config with a dynamic `_subdirectory` and every template's questions `when:`-gated in that single file, which stops per-template question schemas from being self-contained artifacts.

The bundled `project` and `streamlit` templates version independently inside the Boilerplate repository, so they do not resolve to their own repositories; release-time extraction into per-template repositories is the design in [ADR-006](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-006-template-distribution/index.md), and the catalog-monorepo convention for aggregating independently versioned template repositories as submodules is in [Design — Template system § Submodule Federation and Tool Ownership](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/03-template-system/#submodule-federation-and-tool-ownership).

## Composition constraints

Templates declare dependencies via `extends`:

```yaml
# boilerplate.yml (streamlit template)
version: "0.2.0"
name: streamlit
extends:
  - project  # unversioned reference: the latest registered project template
```

A breaking change in a base template, and how it propagates through the templates that extend it, is specified in [Design — Project lifecycle § Structural changes to the `extends` chain](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/06-project-lifecycle/#step-3-build-updateplan) and the `UpdatePlan`/`LayerChange` fields in [Design — Data models](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/02-data-models/#updateplan).

## Template author responsibilities

### Before adding breaking changes

1. **Consider Alternatives**
1. Can the change be non-breaking?
1. Can it be added as optional new variable?
1. **Plan Migration**
1. Write Copier migration scripts
1. Test with real projects
1. Document what changed
1. **Check Dependents**
1. If other templates extend this template, bump their version too
1. Update their `extends` constraint
1. Provide their migration scripts

### For each breaking change

- Bump MAJOR version (e.g., 1.0.0 → 2.0.0)
- Add the migration to `_migrations` in `copier.yml`
- Test migration with `copier update` on sample projects
- Update referenced templates' `extends` constraints
- Document migration in migration guide (see [Migration guide template](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/migration-guide-template/index.md))
- Update template documentation

### Example: renaming a template variable

Renaming a template variable (for example, `project_name` → `project_id`) bumps the major version, then ships a migration that:

- Renames the key in the layer's `.copier-answers.<layer>.yml`
- Finds and replaces the old variable name across generated files
- Updates the question definition in `copier.yml`

See Copier's [migrations documentation](https://copier.readthedocs.io/en/stable/configuring/#migrations) for the mechanism.

## Deprecation vs. breaking changes

### Features being removed (deprecation required)

Deprecation applies when removing template features with **no automated migration path**:

```text
v1.0.0: Feature works normally
v1.1.0: Feature deprecated (still works, warning in docs)
v2.0.0: Feature removed (no migration script exists)
```

Deprecation period: **At least one minor version**.

### Breaking changes (with automated migration)

Template breaking changes accompanied by Copier migrations **do not require a deprecation period**:

```text
v1.0.0: Old structure (e.g., config.yml at root)
v2.0.0: New structure (config.yml in .boilerplate/)
        + Copier migration script handles the move
        → Users update with copier update (automatic migration)
```

**Rationale**: Copier's three-way merge system preserves user customizations during updates.

See [Versioning & compatibility policy § When to choose each path](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/governance/versioning/#when-to-choose-each-path) for the distinction between template and CLI breaking changes.

## Migration guide documentation

See [Migration guide template](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/migration-guide-template/index.md) for required format. Migration guides document:

- What template changed
- Why it changed
- What migration does automatically
- What requires manual intervention (if any)
- Validation procedures

## Testing template migrations

### Test suite requirements

A migration test does three things:

- Create a project from the previous template version.
- Run `copier update` against the new version.
- Assert the migration's effect on the resulting tree — renamed or moved files exist at their new paths, and a project edit to the old path survives as a merge conflict rather than a silent deletion.

`tests/boilerplate/templates/test_streamlit_update_migration.py` drives exactly this against the streamlit layer's smoke-test rename and is the worked example for a new migration test.

## Terminology

[Template](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-template), [Question](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-question), [Copier](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-copier), [`copier.yml`](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-copier-yml), and [`boilerplate.yml`](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-boilerplate-yml) follow the definitions in [design 01's glossary](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#glossary). A "template variable" above is a **Question**. Migration-specific terms used on this page:

**Copier Migration**: An entry under `_migrations` in `copier.yml` — a command, gated by an optional `version` and `when` — that transforms a rendered project during `copier update`.

**Extends**: A dependency on a base template, pinned to an exact version (e.g., `project@1.0.0`) or left unversioned.

**Migration-First**: The principle that a breaking change is acceptable when an automated Copier migration handles it.

**Three-Way Merge**: Copier's merge algorithm, combining old template files, the user's customized project files, and new template files into a result that preserves user customizations.

## Where next

Authoring a template that will need to version and migrate? Start with the [Template authoring guide](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/authoring/index.md), draft the change with the [Migration guide template](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/migration-guide-template/index.md), and check whether it also needs a CLI-side deprecation path in the [Versioning & compatibility policy](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/governance/versioning/index.md). The target machinery this page prepares for — `BoilerplateLock` and `UpdatePlan` in [Design — Data models](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/02-data-models/index.md), the `extends` syntax and submodule federation in [Design — Template system](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/03-template-system/index.md), structural `extends`-chain changes in [Design — Project lifecycle](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/06-project-lifecycle/index.md), and the update orchestration in [ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md) — is where the rest of the story lives.

# Streamlit template

The Streamlit template creates a Streamlit app, built on the [general-purpose template](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/project/index.md). The app reads its own project's `uv.lock` and shows the stack it runs on, with container deployment included.

## Features

- Stack inventory dashboard: locked package count, runtime vs. development vs. transitive dependencies, and the packages the most others depend on — no network, sample data, or fixtures needed at runtime.
- Layered architecture: models validate, services compute, an adapter reads the lock file, and `app.py` only renders.
- A unit test module per layer, plus a Streamlit `AppTest` that drives the rendered page.
- VS Code debugger configuration — press `F5` to run the app under the debugger.
- Container deployment: a Dockerfile and build/push scripts that work with whichever registry you answered at generation time.

## Project structure

```text
my-streamlit-app/
├── pyproject.toml          # Project configuration
├── README.md               # App documentation
├── uv.lock                 # Dependencies
├── Dockerfile              # Multi-stage container definition
├── .dockerignore
├── .copier-answers.project.yml    # The project layer's answers, for future updates
├── .copier-answers.streamlit.yml  # This layer's answers, for future updates
├── boilerplate.lock        # Each layer's version, source and checksum
├── .vscode/
│   ├── settings.json       # Workspace settings (inherited from project)
│   ├── extensions.json     # Recommended extensions (inherited from project)
│   └── launch.json         # Debugger configuration
├── scripts/
│   ├── build-container.sh  # Container build script
│   └── push-container.sh   # Registry push script
├── src/
│   └── my_streamlit_app/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── app.py              # Widgets and layout only
│       ├── adapters/
│       │   ├── __init__.py
│       │   └── lockfile.py     # Reads uv.lock with tomllib, returns validated models
│       ├── models/
│       │   ├── __init__.py
│       │   ├── locked_package.py
│       │   ├── project_info.py
│       │   ├── stack_filter.py
│       │   ├── stack_row.py
│       │   └── stack_summary.py
│       └── services/
│           ├── __init__.py
│           └── inventory.py    # Pure functions: classify, filter, summarize
└── tests/
    ├── my_streamlit_app/
    │   ├── adapters/test_lockfile.py
    │   ├── models/
    │   │   ├── test_locked_package.py
    │   │   └── test_stack_filter.py
    │   ├── services/test_inventory.py
    │   └── test_import.py      # Checks the package imports (from project)
    └── integration/
        └── my_streamlit_app/
            └── test_app.py      # Drives the page with Streamlit's AppTest
```

The package name derives from the project name. The render also inherits the project template's `notebooks/`, `.vscode/`, `.gitignore`, and `tests/<package>/test_import.py`; the base layer's sample module stays off, and the import test renders in its place, because this template answers `sample_module` with no. Each layer records its answers in its own `.copier-answers.<layer>.yml`.

`README.md`, `src/<package>/app.py` and `tests/integration/<package>/test_app.py` are project-owned: the template lists them in `_skip_if_exists`, which [governs what an update does to them](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/04-composition-engine/#per-layer-render-loop).

A project rendered by an earlier 0.1 release of this layer carries the smoke test as `tests_app.py`. On update, a before-stage migration moves it to `test_app.py` with `git mv`, so the update presents the file as a conflict holding both versions instead of deleting yours. This layer declares only its own questions and takes the rest from `project` through the composition, so updating it needs the merged schema that `boilerplate update` will provide ([ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md) records that design); a plain `copier update` of a copy of the layer rendered from a git repository exits 0 while skipping every path under the package directory, and [Update a git-backed layer](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/plain-copier/#update-a-git-backed-layer) shows the flags that update it by hand. The copy bundled in the package cannot update with plain Copier at all ([copy-only](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/plain-copier/#bundled-layers-are-copy-only)). Copier requires `--trust` for an update that runs a migration. With `--no-tasks`, the inherited cleanup task never runs either, so `_scripts/post_generation.py` (from the `project` layer) is left behind and isn't gitignored.

## Usage

```bash
# Create new Streamlit app (template name, then destination)
boilerplate new streamlit ./my-data-app
cd my-data-app

# Run the app locally (package name derives from the project name)
uv run streamlit run src/my_data_app/app.py
```

The inherited post-generation tasks already ran `uv sync`. If you passed `--no-tasks`, run `uv sync` before the first `uv run`.

For container deployment, see [container deployment](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/index.md).

## Development

### Architecture

The template follows a layered architecture:

- **Models** (`models/`): Pydantic models that validate the lock file's contents and the UI's widget values.
- **Services** (`services/`): pure functions over the models — no I/O, no Streamlit import.
- **Adapters** (`adapters/`): I/O — reads `uv.lock` and returns validated models.
- **App** (`app.py`): the Streamlit UI — widgets, layout, and calls into services and the adapter.

Condensed from the template's `adapters/lockfile.py`, `models/locked_package.py`, `services/inventory.py`, and `app.py` (imports, docstrings, and the adapter's parsing body trimmed — the rendered files are complete):

```python
# adapters/lockfile.py
def read_lockfile(path: Path) -> tuple[ProjectInfo, tuple[LockedPackage, ...]]:
    data = tomllib.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    # ... locate the root package, build ProjectInfo and every LockedPackage
    return project, packages

# models/locked_package.py
class LockedPackage(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)
    name: str
    version: str
    source_kind: str
    dependencies: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# services/inventory.py
def build_rows(
    project: ProjectInfo, packages: Sequence[LockedPackage]
) -> tuple[StackRow, ...]:
    dependent_counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for package in packages:
        for dependency in package.dependencies:
            dependent_counts[dependency] = dependent_counts.get(dependency, 0) + 1

    rows = [
        StackRow(
            name=package.name,
            version=package.version,
            scope=_scope_of(package.name, project),
            source_kind=package.source_kind,
            dependents=dependent_counts.get(package.name, 0),
        )
        for package in packages
        if package.name != project.name
    ]
    return tuple(sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row.name))

# app.py
project, packages = read_lockfile(LOCKFILE)
rows = build_rows(project, packages)
stack_filter = StackFilter.model_validate({"search": search, "scope": scope, "limit": limit})
st.dataframe([row.model_dump() for row in apply_filter(rows, stack_filter)], hide_index=True)
```

### Debugging

Press `F5` in VS Code to launch the Streamlit app with the debugger attached. The `.vscode/launch.json` is pre-configured.

## Tests

- `test_locked_package.py`: PEP 503 name normalization.
- `test_stack_filter.py`: widget-value validation — search pattern, scope, and limit bounds.
- `test_lockfile.py`: parses a lock file into `ProjectInfo` and `LockedPackage`; raises on a missing root package or a missing file.
- `test_inventory.py`: classification into runtime, dev, and transitive; dependent counts; filtering; summarizing.
- `test_app.py` (integration): drives the rendered page with Streamlit's `AppTest` — runs without exception, shows the correct locked-package count, and warns on invalid filter input.

# Deploying Streamlit containers

Every render ships a Dockerfile and two scripts — `scripts/build-container.sh` and `scripts/push-container.sh` — that build and publish a container image. This section covers each part of the process; every script step also has a manual equivalent.

## Overview

The scripts run on any Docker host: Linux, macOS or Windows with Docker Desktop, or WSL2 on Windows. [Environment setup](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/environment-setup/index.md) covers the WSL2 case.

Once an image is built, running it locally always looks the same:

```bash
docker run -p 8501:8501 text-highlighter:local
```

## What you'll learn

- How to prepare your machine for containerized Streamlit deployment.
- How to build Docker images from your Streamlit project.
- How to push those images to GitHub Container Registry, Azure Container Registry, or any other registry you're already logged into.

Don't add yourself to the `docker` group

Running Docker without `sudo` requires membership in the `docker` group, which grants root-level access via the Docker socket. The build and push scripts detect whether your session can already reach Docker and fall back to `sudo` otherwise, so you never need that group membership just to run them.

## Topics

- [Environment setup](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/environment-setup/index.md) Install Docker and `uv`, plus the Azure CLI if you push to Azure Container Registry or build against an Azure DevOps package index.
- [Building container images](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/building-container-images/index.md) Build an image with the script or manual `docker buildx` commands; authenticate to a private package index when your project uses one.
- [Pushing container images](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/pushing-container-images/index.md) Publish the image to GitHub Container Registry, Azure Container Registry, or another registry, using the script or manual `docker` commands.

# Building container images

Build a Docker image from your Streamlit project using either the included script or manual `docker buildx` commands.

## Requirements

Before you begin:

- Docker, reachable directly or via `sudo` — [Environment setup](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/environment-setup/index.md) covers installing it, including on WSL2.
- Your project must include:
  - A `pyproject.toml` file with a `[project] name` field.
  - A `uv.lock` file for dependency resolution.

If your project's package index (the `package_index_url` answer from generation time) is empty, that's everything you need. If it points at a private index, see [Private package index](#private-package-index) below.

## Build options

You can use the provided script to streamline the build process or follow the manual steps below.

### Use the build script

Run the build script from your project directory:

```bash
./scripts/build-container.sh
```

This script will:

- Validate the presence of `uv.lock` (and read `pyproject.toml` to derive the default image name).
- Use `docker` directly if your session can reach the daemon, or `sudo docker` otherwise.
- Build the image with `docker buildx`. When your project has a private package index configured, it authenticates first — see [Private package index](#private-package-index).
- Tag the image using the project name with a default `:local` tag.

If your `pyproject.toml` includes:

```toml
[project]
name = "text-highlighter"
```

The resulting image will be:

```text
text-highlighter:local
```

Upon successful completion, you'll see:

```text
✅ Docker image built successfully: text-highlighter:local
ℹ️  To run your container locally:
   docker run -p 8501:8501 text-highlighter:local
📣  Note: If your app runs on a different port, update the -p flag accordingly.
```

### Build manually

With no private package index, the script's build step is one command:

```bash
docker buildx build --tag text-highlighter:local --load .
```

Prefix it with `sudo` if your Docker daemon needs that. Replace `text-highlighter:local` with your preferred image tag.

## Private package index

When your project's package index needs credentials, the build passes them to `uv sync` as a Docker secret (`id=index`) so they never land in an image layer — the Dockerfile's `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=index,env=INDEX uv sync --default-index "$INDEX" --keyring-provider subprocess` consumes it. Which credentials, and how the script gets them, depends on the index host.

### Azure DevOps index

When the index host is `dev.azure.com` or `pkgs.visualstudio.com`, the script requests a short-lived Azure DevOps token through the Azure CLI and passes it as the secret. You need `az` installed and available on `PATH`.

Manual steps:

1. Authenticate with Azure CLI

   ```bash
   az login
   ```

1. Retrieve a short-lived Azure DevOps token

   ```bash
   TOKEN=$(az account get-access-token \
     --resource 499b84ac-1321-427f-aa17-267ca6975798 \
     --query accessToken -o tsv)
   ```

1. Build the Docker image

   ```bash
   INDEX="https://AzureDevOps:${TOKEN}@<your-feed>/simple/" \
   docker buildx build \
     --secret id=index,env=INDEX \
     --tag text-highlighter:local \
     --load .
   ```

### Any other private index

Set `INDEX_URL` to the index URL with credentials embedded (for example `https://user:token@host/simple/`) before running the script; the script errors with this instruction if it's unset:

```bash
INDEX_URL="https://user:token@host/simple/" ./scripts/build-container.sh
```

Manually, pass the same value through as the build secret:

```bash
env INDEX="$INDEX_URL" docker buildx build \
  --secret id=index,env=INDEX \
  --tag text-highlighter:local \
  --load .
```

## Verifying the image

After building, confirm that your image exists:

```bash
docker images
```

To test it locally:

```bash
docker run -p 8501:8501 text-highlighter:local
```

Change the `-p` value if your application serves on a different port.

## Where next

[Continue to pushing container images](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/pushing-container-images/index.md), or return to the [container deployment overview](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/index.md).

# Environment setup

Install the tools needed to build and deploy containerized applications from your WSL2 Ubuntu environment. Choose between a fully automated setup script or manual installation.

## Platform setup (one-time)

If you're setting up WSL2 for the first time, open PowerShell as Administrator and run:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

This installs:

- Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2)
- Ubuntu (default distribution)
- Required virtualization components

After installation, restart your machine and launch Ubuntu from the Start Menu to complete setup.

## Setup options

The build and push scripts use `docker` directly when your session can already reach the daemon, and fall back to `sudo docker` otherwise — see the [Docker security note](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/index.md) for why staying out of the `docker` group is worth it.

Choose one of the following methods to install the required tools inside your WSL2 Ubuntu environment.

### Automated setup (recommended)

The setup script ships in the [boilerplate repository](https://github.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate/blob/main/scripts/setup-wsl-env.sh), not in your generated project — download it first, then run it in your Ubuntu terminal:

```bash
curl -O \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TheRealBillSiegler/boilerplate/main/scripts/setup-wsl-env.sh
chmod +x setup-wsl-env.sh
./setup-wsl-env.sh
```

This installs:

- Docker CE (from Docker's official APT repository)
- Azure CLI (from Microsoft's APT repository). The script always installs it; you only need it for Azure Container Registry pushes or an Azure DevOps package index. If neither applies, use the manual setup below and skip the Azure CLI section.
- uv (from Astral's installer)

Example usage:

```bash
sudo docker run hello-world
```

### Manual setup

If you prefer to install dependencies manually, use the commands below.

#### Docker CE

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg lsb-release apt-transport-https

sudo mkdir -m 0755 -p /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg |
sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg

echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) \
signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] \
https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu \
$(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" |
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y \
  docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin \
  docker-compose-plugin
```

#### Azure CLI

Only needed for pushing to Azure Container Registry or building against an Azure DevOps package index — skip this section otherwise.

```bash
curl -sL https://packages.microsoft.com/keys/microsoft.asc |
gpg --dearmor |
sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/microsoft.gpg > /dev/null

AZ_REPO=$(lsb_release -cs)
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) \
signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/microsoft.gpg] \
https://packages.microsoft.com/repos/azure-cli/ $AZ_REPO main" |
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/azure-cli.list

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y azure-cli
```

#### uv

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
uv --version
```

[Continue to building container images](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/building-container-images/index.md), or return to the [container deployment overview](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/index.md).

# Pushing container images

Push a local Docker image to a registry using the included script or manual `docker` commands. Authentication depends on which registry you push to.

## Requirements

Before pushing, ensure:

- You've already built a local Docker image (see [Building container images](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/building-container-images/index.md)).
- Docker is reachable, directly or via `sudo`.

## Push options

You can use the provided script to streamline the push process or push the image manually.

### Use the push script

Run the script from your project directory:

```bash
./scripts/push-container.sh
```

Options:

- `-i`/`--image-name` — local image (default `<project-name>:local`).
- `-r`/`--registry` — registry hostname (default the `container_registry` answer from generation time).
- `-n`/`--namespace` — owner or organization within the registry (default `$CONTAINER_NAMESPACE`, else empty).
- `-t`/`--tag` — remote tag (default `latest`).

The remote name is `<registry>/<namespace>/<repo>:<tag>` when a namespace is set, otherwise `<registry>/<repo>:<tag>`:

```bash
./scripts/push-container.sh \
  --image-name text-highlighter:local \
  --registry ghcr.io \
  --namespace my-org \
  --tag prod
```

Authentication is chosen from the registry hostname at push time, so the same script keeps working if you change registries later.

### GitHub Container Registry and Docker Hub

`--namespace` is required — it's the owner or organization the image belongs to; the script exits with an error if it's missing. If `REGISTRY_TOKEN` is set, the script signs in with it (`docker login ghcr.io --username <namespace> --password-stdin`); otherwise it assumes you already ran `docker login ghcr.io` and continues. New packages on GHCR are private until you make them public in the package's settings on GitHub — that switch can't be undone. Docker Hub (`docker.io`) follows the same rules: `--namespace` is required and `REGISTRY_TOKEN` signs you in.

### Azure Container Registry

No namespace needed. The script requires the Azure CLI, checks `az account show` and runs `az login` if you're signed out, then acquires a short-lived Microsoft Entra ID access token with `az acr login --expose-token` and logs Docker in with it.

### Any other registry

The script assumes you're already signed in (`docker login <registry>`) and continues.

### Push manually

**GitHub Container Registry:**

```bash
echo "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io \
  --username <owner> \
  --password-stdin   # skip if you already ran `docker login ghcr.io`

docker tag text-highlighter:local ghcr.io/<owner>/text-highlighter:latest
docker push ghcr.io/<owner>/text-highlighter:latest
```

**Azure Container Registry:**

```bash
az login

TOKEN=$(az acr login \
  --name <your-registry> \
  --expose-token \
  --query accessToken -o tsv)

echo "$TOKEN" | docker login <your-registry>.azurecr.io \
  --username 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 \
  --password-stdin

docker tag text-highlighter:local <your-registry>.azurecr.io/text-highlighter:latest
docker push <your-registry>.azurecr.io/text-highlighter:latest
```

**Any other registry:**

```bash
docker login <registry>   # once, if not already signed in
docker tag text-highlighter:local <registry>/text-highlighter:latest
docker push <registry>/text-highlighter:latest
```

Prefix any `docker` command above with `sudo` if your daemon needs it.

## Verifying the push

GitHub Container Registry lists the image under the owner's or organization's Packages tab. Azure Container Registry lists it with:

```bash
az acr repository show-tags \
  --name <your-registry> \
  --repository text-highlighter
```

For any other registry, check its own UI or API.

## Discover templates

- List the templates you can create a project from:

```powershell
boilerplate list
```

```text
  Name        Version   Description

  project     0.3.0     A general-purpose Python project, with its tools configured.

## Create a new project

- Latest project template into a new folder:

```

## Inspect a template graph

- Text tree format (the `streamlit` template extends `project`, so its graph shows the chain):

```powershell
boilerplate graph streamlit --format tree
```

```text
- streamlit@0.2.0
  - project@0.3.0
```

- JSON written to file:

```powershell
boilerplate graph streamlit --format json -o graph.json
```

The JSON payload's shape (the `streamlit` template extends `project`, so its graph has two layers):

```json
{
  "sequence": [
    "project@0.3.0",
    "streamlit@0.2.0"
  ],
  "layers": [
    {
      "specifier": "project@0.3.0",
      "name": "project",
      "version": "0.3.0",
      "path": ".../templates/project",
      "deps": []
    },
    {
      "specifier": "streamlit@0.2.0",
      "name": "streamlit",
      "version": "0.2.0",
      "path": ".../templates/streamlit",
      "deps": ["project@0.3.0"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Compose a template

- Show final merged questions and the per-layer contributions:

```powershell

```

- Export all major sections to a directory and stay quiet:

```powershell
boilerplate compose project --all -o out --quiet
```

- Quick shape check with the stats section:

# Customization

Every template — current and future — can be customized three ways, ordered by power. Reach for the least powerful mechanism that works:

| You want to…                                                          | Use                                             | Grain     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| Set a value stamped into output (an index URL, a registry, your name) | **Profile** (`profile.toml`)                    | a value   |
| Add or replace whole files, shareably                                 | a **layer** — a template that `extends` another | structure |
| Anything else (edit files a template never anticipated)               | **your own script** after `boilerplate new`     | behavior  |

## Profile (`profile.toml`)

Create `profile.toml` in the boilerplate config directory (`%APPDATA%\boilerplate\` on Windows; `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/boilerplate/` or `~/.config/boilerplate/` elsewhere):

```toml
[defaults]                      # fills a matching question in ANY template
author_name = "Jane Dev"
package_index_url = "https://pkgs.example.com/org/_packaging/feed/pypi/simple/"

[templates.streamlit]           # only for this template; overrides [defaults]
container_registry = "myregistry.azurecr.io"
```

- Keys are **template question names** (see each template's `copier.yml`). The only reserved names are the two table headers; a key matching no question is ignored.
- Precedence, high to low: your interactive answer › `[templates.<name>]` › `[defaults]` › the template's own default. Defaults pre-fill prompts — you can still override at the prompt; `--non-interactive` takes them as-is.

### Questions the first-party templates share

| Question                       | Templates                             | Effect                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `package_index_url`            | `project` and everything extending it | emits a default `[[tool.uv.index]]` block in the generated `pyproject.toml` (empty = public PyPI, no block)                                                                                                                                                                |
| `sample_module`                | `project` and everything extending it | renders `module.py` and its test (default on; off renders `test_import.py` instead; a layer that extends `project` can default it off)                                                                                                                                     |
| `build_backend`                | `project` and everything extending it | build backend in the generated `pyproject.toml`: `uv_build` (default) or `hatchling`, which also renders the `[tool.hatch]` wheel table — see [Choose a build backend](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/project/#choose-a-build-backend) |
| `container_registry`           | `streamlit`                           | registry used by the generated `push-container.sh`; authentication is chosen by registry hostname — see [Pushing container images](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/streamlit/deployment/containers/pushing-container-images/index.md)   |
| `author_name` / `author_email` | `project` and everything extending it | project metadata                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

## Layers (structure)

Need files a template doesn't ship? Author a template that `extends` it and add them — composition merges files, questions, and tasks:

```yaml
# my-org-project/boilerplate.yml
schema_version: "1"
name: org-project
version: 0.1.0
description: Org house style on top of the general-purpose template.
extends: [project]
```

The folder also needs a `copier.yml`; template discovery skips a folder that lacks either file.

Point boilerplate at its parent directory with `--templates-dir` (or set the `BOILERPLATE_EXTRA_TEMPLATE_DIRS` environment variable — a JSON list of paths, e.g. `BOILERPLATE_EXTRA_TEMPLATE_DIRS='["C:/my/templates"]'`, in the environment or a `.env` file in the working directory; a bare path string is rejected) and run `boilerplate new org-project`. The option adds to the search path rather than replacing it, so bundled templates like `project` stay resolvable for `extends`. Your layer applies when you create a project; carrying later changes from `project` into projects you've already made is planned.

## Your own script (behavior)

For anything neither values nor layers cover — appending to a generated file, registering the project somewhere — run your own script after generation:

```powershell
boilerplate new project my-app
./my-post-gen.ps1 my-app
```

Boilerplate deliberately does not manage these scripts.

## The org pattern

An organization's customization is **two plain files delivered by one org-owned script**, run once per developer machine after the canonical installer:

1. `uv.toml` — points the *machine's* package resolution at the org feed (plus credential tooling such as `keyring`). This is uv configuration, not boilerplate's.
1. `profile.toml` — the org's generation defaults (above).

A reference script an org can adapt (fictional `acme` names):

```powershell
#Requires -Version 7
# acme-setup.ps1 — run AFTER the public boilerplate installer.
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

# 1. Machine package resolution: authenticated org feed for uv.
uv tool install keyring --with artifacts-keyring
$UvDir = Join-Path $env:APPDATA 'uv'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $UvDir | Out-Null
@'
keyring-provider = "subprocess"
publish-url = "https://pkgs.example.com/acme/_packaging/feed/pypi/upload/"
check-url = "https://VssSessionToken@pkgs.example.com/acme/_packaging/feed/pypi/simple/"

[[index]]
name = "acme"
url = "https://VssSessionToken@pkgs.example.com/acme/_packaging/feed/pypi/simple/"
default = true
'@ | Set-Content (Join-Path $UvDir 'uv.toml') -Encoding utf8

# 2. Generation defaults: stamped into every project the developer creates.
$BpDir = Join-Path $env:APPDATA 'boilerplate'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $BpDir | Out-Null
@'
[defaults]
package_index_url = "https://pkgs.example.com/acme/_packaging/feed/pypi/simple/"

[templates.streamlit]
container_registry = "acme.azurecr.io"
'@ | Set-Content (Join-Path $BpDir 'profile.toml') -Encoding utf8

Write-Host "Acme configuration applied."
```

Hosting, verifying, and updating that script is the org's business — the same trust boundary as the rest of its machine setup. Note the script overwrites any personal `profile.toml`; on org machines that is usually what you want.
