- **The scoped view held in the fields of a `Worker` subclass (chosen)** — the layer keeps its own `copier.yml` free of the join, Copier runs every render, and the view reaches all three of Copier's update renders.
- **Every render under the full merged schema** — rejected: a descendant's context hook rewrote an ancestor's rendered files, and every answers file recorded siblings' answers ([Verification (2026-10-06)](#verification-2026-10-06)).
- **The scoped view alone as the source of question definitions and defaults at update** — rejected: an ancestor's update recorded the ancestor's own default for a new question its descendant overrides, in both walk orders ([Verification (2026-10-06)](#verification-2026-10-06)); the step takes definitions and defaults from the full merged schema instead.
- **A later layer's recorded value over an earlier one's** — rejected: passed data outranks the answers file in Copier's answer precedence (`AnswersMap.combined`), so a descendant's stale copy of an ancestor's answer, passed over the ancestor's, would shadow the value the ancestor's migration wrote.
- **One questionnaire pass before the walk** — rejected: it asks for questions a migration answers, and a renamed question's default overrode the migrated answer in both layers and both orders ([Verification (2026-10-08)](#verification-2026-10-08)).
- **A file-path extension registered once, from one source at the target versions** — rejected: the old copy renders with the new code, so the update silently keeps the old output ([Verification (2026-10-06)](#verification-2026-10-06)).
- **A merged template set on one worker instance** — rejected: `dataclasses.replace` rebuilds the update renders without it ([Verification (2026-09-30)](#verification-2026-09-30)).
- **Declaring inherited questions in each child layer so a vanilla per-layer update sees them** — rejected: it duplicates the parent's schema by hand, and the copy drifts when the parent renames or retypes the question.
- **A Boilerplate-shipped context hook in each layer's `_jinja_extensions` that persists inherited answers into the answers file** — rejected as the primary mechanism and kept as the runner-up: it updated cleanly in 8 updates across both orders and it also heals the hand-run hatch, but the template then ships the join mechanism, and the hook writes secret answers in clear text unless it filters them.
- **Carrying inherited answers through the child's answers-file stub with `combine`** — rejected: it shares the hook's objection, and a stub cannot carry derived answers for projects that never recorded them.
- **Passing data to a vanilla update with `--data-file`** — retained as the hand-run hatch with the limits in point 1, because the old render never sees passed data.
- **Asking `project_slug` and `package_name` as regular questions so the answers files record them** — open: it would heal the hand-run hatch for child layers at the cost of two more compose-time prompts, and the project team has not decided it.

## Consequences

- A project carrying a single canonical `.copier-answers.yml` is a migration item; adoption accepts the legacy singular shape beside per-layer files ([design 06](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/06-project-lifecycle/index.md)).
- The per-layer answers file is the distribution contract: whatever `_src_path` and `_commit` record must stay resolvable by vanilla Copier, on any machine, indefinitely. The distribution consequences are owned by [ADR-006](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-006-template-distribution/index.md).
- Non-git layers do not update (point 5): they are skipped with a warning, and `copier recopy` is the Copier-idiomatic refresh for such a layer when the user wants one. [ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md)'s per-layer update model follows this.
- Passages of the target corpus this decision binds: the non-git-layer glossary entry ([01](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-non-git-layer)); the `--no-base` / two-way-comparison passages ([05](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/05-cli-reference/index.md), [06](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/06-project-lifecycle/index.md)); the trust tables ([02](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/02-data-models/index.md), [03](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/03-template-system/index.md), [09](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/09-settings-and-configuration/index.md)), which name `wheel_bundle` as the trusted first-party mechanism — what replaces it depends on the open question [ADR-003](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-003-permissive-execution/index.md) owns, since first-party templates arriving over the network meet ADR-003's own stated trigger for tightening; this ADR does not settle it; the `LockLayer.source_bundle` / `subdirectory` fields ([02](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/02-data-models/index.md)); and INT-001's `_subdirectory` expectation.

## Verification (2026-07-28)

Empirical run against Copier 9.15.0 (Windows, git 2.55, `core.autocrlf=true`): stacked two-template fixtures (base plus an overlay overwriting a base-rendered file), per-layer answers files, vanilla `copier` CLI only — six scenarios plus an independent adversarial re-run with differently shaped fixtures.

- **Survival confirmed.** Updating the base while its diff is disjoint from the overlay's overwrite leaves the overlay's content intact and the other layer's answers file hash-identical; the updated layer's answers file advances to the new tag.
- **Collision pause confirmed.** When the base update changes a file the overlay overwrote, Copier writes inline conflict markers (`<<<<<<< before updating` / `>>>>>>> after updating`) with the overlay's content preserved on the "before" side and git reporting unmerged paths — never a silent revert, in both a line-edit and a whole-file-rewrite variant.
- **Overlay independence confirmed.** Updating the overlay layer alone lands its changes and leaves base-rendered files and the base answers file hash-identical.
- **Plain-directory degradation confirmed.** Copy from a non-git directory succeeds and records no `_commit`; `copier update` against that layer fails specifically ("Cannot update because cannot obtain old template references", exit 1) — there is no built-in two-way fallback — while the git-backed layer beside it stays fully updatable.
- **Dirty-HEAD author loop confirmed.** `--vcs-ref=HEAD` includes uncommitted template changes (with `DirtyLocalWarning`) and records a `git describe`-shaped `_commit` (`v1.0.0-1-g<hash>`); without the flag, the latest tag renders clean. That hash names the automated draft commit Copier makes inside its own throwaway clone, so it exists in no repository afterwards: a dirty-HEAD render is an authoring convenience, never a provenance record, and `new` MUST NOT use it.

Caveats the run surfaced, now part of the record:

- **The `_answers_file:` directive is inert without a stub.** Copier writes an answers file only by rendering a template-shipped `{{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja`; a template lacking one composes with exit 0 and silently produces no answers file. Design 04 names both halves of the contract, and a template offered for composition without a stub is copy-only by construction.
- **`copier update` exits 0 with unresolved conflicts in the tree**, and the updated layer's answers file already records the new tag while markers sit unresolved. Orchestration and CI must detect the pause via git unmerged state or a marker scan, never exit codes — this lands on [ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md)'s conflict-pause envelope.
- **Byte-identity must be stated in git's content sense.** With `core.autocrlf=true`, Copier's git-based update rewrites line endings of files it otherwise leaves untouched — content-identical but raw-hash-different, and reported as modified by `git status` in most runs (one run's `git diff` suppressed it, others did not); an `autocrlf=false` control preserved exact bytes. Checksum-based drift detection must normalize line endings, and "unchanged" must never be asserted from `git status` alone.
- **Small files conflict more than edit-distance intuition suggests.** On a three-line file, a template edit and a user append at opposite ends still conflict, because the diff hunk's context spans the whole file. The pause is honest; "non-overlapping edits merge cleanly" holds only for files larger than the diff context window.
- **Compose-time ref pinning is mandatory.** Bare `copier copy` resolves the latest tag, so layer application must pin `--vcs-ref` per the resolved specifier (Boilerplate's version resolution already provides the pin).

## Verification (2026-09-04)

Empirical run against the bundled `project` and `streamlit` templates (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, git 2.55): each template copied into a local git repository and tagged; a project composed by `boilerplate new` from the wheel's plain directories, then rehomed by editing each answers file's `_src_path` to the clone and adding `_commit`; vanilla `copier update -a .copier-answers.<layer>.yml` per layer after tagging a new version of each template, in both orders.

- **Real-template defects found.** `project` declared `_exclude: [_extensions]`, which replaces Copier's default exclusions rather than extending them, so the update copied the clone's `.git` over the project's own (the engine reinstates the defaults at compose; vanilla Copier does not). `streamlit`'s files and paths used `package_name`, `project_name`, and `package_index_url` without declaring them, so its vanilla per-layer re-render, which sees only the layer's own `copier.yml`, produced a different Dockerfile and the update paused on a conflict no edit had caused. For the rest of the run, `project` restated the default exclusions and `streamlit` declared those questions.
- **With those fixes, both layers updated cleanly in either order.** The changed layer's answers file advanced to the new tag, the other layer's file stayed hash-identical, and new files and edits landed without conflict.
- **A vanilla per-layer update drops foreign keys on its first rewrite.** The project layer's answers file lost `container_registry` on its first update.
- **The vanilla update needed Boilerplate importable.** `project`'s `_jinja_extensions` imports a filter from the `boilerplate` package. `boilerplate new` could not compose from git-backed template directories at the time of the run, which is why the run rehomed the answers files by hand.

## Verification (2026-09-30)

Empirical run against the bundled `project` and `streamlit` templates (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, local git clones, `--defaults`, `skip_tasks`): `streamlit/copier.yml` reduced to its own questions and overrides (`dependencies`, `sample_module`, `container_registry`), both layers cloned into tagged git repositories, a project composed by `boilerplate new` and rehomed to the clones with `_commit: v1` (the 2026-09-04 recipe). Each new tag edited the README line that renders `project_name` and appended a file that renders seven inherited answers, five recorded and two derived; a user line appended to the README before the first update had to survive.

- **A `Worker` subclass holding the merged view updated cleanly.** Copier's `update`, run per layer through a subclass that holds the merged questions and the extension union in fields and builds `template` from them, with `data=` the union of the per-layer answers files (the merge order of the union was not recorded), exited 0 on all 8 updates in both orders (project then streamlit, streamlit then project; v2 then v3). Copier left no conflict markers, no `.rej` files and no unmerged paths, and it persisted all five inherited answers in `streamlit`'s answers file after every update. The derived values rendered (`widget_co`, `widget-co`), the package directory stayed intact and the user line survived.
- **A template set on the worker instance lost the inherited answers.** Copier's `update`, with `worker.template` set to the merged template on one instance, exited 0 on the first `streamlit` update in both orders and dropped all five inherited answers from the answers file. The derived values rendered empty, and the second update paused with conflict markers in `README.md` and the probe file.
- **The hand-run hatch kept the user's work and paused on derived answers.** After two engine updates, `copier update -a .copier-answers.streamlit.yml --defaults --trust --data-file .copier-answers.project.yml --data package_name=widget_co --data project_slug=widget-co`, with a template edit on a far line only, exited 0 in one run, left no `.rej` file, kept the user line and the package directory, and rendered the new line. The file that renders derived answers paused with a conflict marker, because the old render cannot compute derived answers when no answers file records them, and Copier trimmed the answers file to the layer's own keys.
- **Scratch-fixture probes of vanilla updates (2026-09-29 and 2026-09-30) found three limits.** `--data` and `--data-file` rendered the new copy correctly and never reached the old copy, so a template edit on or beside a line that renders a passed-in answer conflicted every time. `_external_data` pointing at another layer's answers file worked at copy and rendered empty on update, because Copier's temporary renders lack the file. An undeclared answer left in an answers file survived one update and rendered empty on the next.

## Verification (2026-10-06)

Empirical run against the bundled `project` and `streamlit` templates and synthetic layers (Copier 9.18.1, Windows, git 2.55): one tagged git repository per layer, every view built by Boilerplate's own Resolver and Composer, and every compose and update run through a `Worker` subclass holding one view per ref, in lock order and in reverse. Every view joined the layer and its ancestors at one shared ref name per step; a view joining independently versioned ancestors was not exercised, and neither was a step whose ancestor moved while the layer's own version did not, the case in which the old copy, the new copy and the in-place render carry one ref and the recorded-versions and target-versions views differ.

- **The full merged schema let a descendant change an ancestor's files.** A `streamlit` context hook that overwrote `description` rewrote `project`'s `pyproject.toml` and package `__init__.py` to the hook's value when every layer rendered under the full merged schema, and `project`'s answers file recorded `streamlit`'s `container_registry`. Under the scoped view, `project` rendered the answered `description` and recorded only its own questions.
- **Each answers file recorded exactly its scoped view.** In a diamond (`docs` extends `project`; `app` extends `streamlit` and `docs`), each answers file recorded its own and its ancestors' questions and no other, and the updates of `docs` and `app` left no conflict markers, no `.rej` files and no unmerged paths. A three-layer chain (`project`, `streamlit`, and a layer extending `streamlit`) updated cleanly in both orders.
- **The questionnaire pass carried a descendant's override of a new ancestor question.** When `project` added `license` (default `MIT`) and `streamlit` overrode its default to `Apache-2.0`, the scoped view with no pass rendered and recorded `MIT` in `project` in both orders, with no error. With one non-interactive pass over the full merged schema at the target versions before the walk, the file and both answers files held `Apache-2.0` in both orders.
- **A file-path extension declared by an ancestor needed registration per layer and ref.** A `streamlit` file using a filter that `project` declares as a file path failed to render with no registration (`No filter named 'probe_shout'`). Registered per layer and ref from `project`'s source at each ref, the update moved the file from the old ref's output to the new ref's with no conflict markers; registered once from one source at the target ref, the old copy rendered with the new code, the old and new copies matched, and the file silently kept the old ref's output with no error. A `streamlit` context hook never reached `project`'s files, at compose or at any update.
- **Copier's update replaced a rejected recorded answer silently.** `project` v2 retyped `port` from `str` to `int`, dropped `GPL-3.0` from a `license` choice list, or added a validator the recorded `author_email` failed. With the recorded answers passed as data, the in-place render's questionnaire raised a `ValueError` before it wrote any file and left the tree and the answers files untouched, while a castable value (`"8080"`) carried over as `8080`. With no data passed, Copier dropped the recorded answer and recorded the new default (`8080`, `MIT`, a valid default address), exited cleanly and printed no warning; a new default that also failed the validator failed the update.
- **Copier ran a layer's tasks three times per update.** With a marker task in `project` and in `streamlit`, compose ran each task once in the destination. A Copier update with tasks enabled ran the updated layer's own task three times, in the old-copy temporary directory, in place and in the new-copy temporary directory, and never ran the other layer's task.
- **Only ancestors-first order carried a renamed question.** `project` v2 renamed `author_name` to `maintainer_name` and shipped a before-stage migration that rewrote the key in its own answers file. In lock order the value carried over in both layers. In reverse order, with the migration in `project` alone, `streamlit`'s update found neither name, recorded the template default `Your Name` with no error or conflict, and kept it after `project`'s later update; with the same migration in `streamlit` too, both orders carried the value.

## Verification (2026-10-08)

Probe scenarios against Copier 9.18.1, on the bundled `project` and `streamlit` templates.

- **A questionnaire pass run before the walk forced a renamed question's default over the migrated answer.** `project` v2 renamed `author_name` to `maintainer_name` behind a before-migration. The pass ran before that migration, found `maintainer_name` unanswered, and its forced default `Your Name` replaced the migrated value in both layers and both orders.

## Relationship to other ADRs

- [ADR-001](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-001-build-vs-adopt/index.md) — "orchestrate, don't reimplement"; Boilerplate drives Copier's own `copy` and `update` per layer and adds one thing, the join: the full merged schema the questionnaire asks, and each layer's scoped view, which reaches every render of that layer through the [ADR-002](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-002-copier-internals-shim/index.md) shim. Boilerplate implements no merge, update or answers-file algorithm of its own.
- [ADR-002](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-002-copier-internals-shim/index.md) — the shim's charter covers compose and update: both run each layer through its scoped view, which is a property of the worker class, and the guard test reports a relocation of `Worker` or `Template` while the version pin bounds the Copier versions both paths run on.
- [ADR-006](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-006-template-distribution/index.md) — distribution must satisfy the answers-file-as-contract constraints.
- [ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md) — the conflict-pause contract is how point 3's collisions surface, and its per-layer update skips non-git layers per point 5.
- [ADR-013](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-013-interactivity-contract/index.md) — the unified prompt flow of point 4 exists only in interactive mode; `--ci`/data-file flows bypass prompting entirely.

# ADR-016: The project vocabulary as one ontology in CONTEXT.md

**Status**: Proposed

> **Scope note.** This ADR fixes how Boilerplate keeps its vocabulary: the names of its concepts, what each one means, how the concepts relate, and where each one lives in files and code. For what exists today, see [status.md](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/status/index.md).

## Context

`CONTEXT.md` at the repository root is the domain glossary. The [design overview's glossary](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#glossary) renders it, and `docs/agents/domain.md` tells the engineering skills to read it before they work in the code. Tenet 14 in `.claude/rules/docs.md` asks for one name per concept, and the glossary's *Avoid* lists name retired synonyms. The vocabulary still drifts in four ways.

- **Copies disagree.** The sweep found the glossary's dev loop entry, the Environment guide and the Quickstart each writing out a different sequence for the same everyday loop.
- **One word names unrelated concepts.**
  - "Profile" names `profile.toml`, a user's default answers, and `EnvironmentProfile` (`boilerplate-env.yml`), the tool versions a project pins. The glossary calls the two "unrelated despite the shared word".
  - "Layer" names a composition layer and, in the key `enforcement_layers` of PROD-001, an enforcement area.
  - "Stack" names the development tools in the brand line, templates building on one another on the home page, and an application's dependencies in the Streamlit template's dashboard.
  - "Workflow" names the general kind of a golden path in the glossary and the reference model, and a GitHub Actions workflow file in the CI guide (`docs/governance/ci.md`).
- **A concept and its file are split in two entries, merged in one, or missing a side.** The glossary separates `EnvironmentProvisionRecord` from `.boilerplate/environment.yml` and the Answers File from `.copier-answers.<layer>.yml`; it merges the lock with `boilerplate.lock` in one entry; it gives `boilerplate.yml` an entry with no template-metadata concept beside it; and it defines Profile by its file.
- **Relations are prose only.** A relation such as "the Toolchain is part of the Development Environment" exists as a sentence, so nothing shows the whole, and a relation to a renamed term goes unnoticed.

Boilerplate's data shapes already have a source of truth: hand-written Pydantic models, such as `BoilerplateLock` and `TemplateMeta` in `src/boilerplate/models/`, and AGENTS.md requires Pydantic at boundaries.

This repository's own history shows what written rules do and do not do ([Verification](#verification-2026-10-18)). A written rule is the specification every check here encodes: each automated check names the prose rule it enforces. A written rule with no check behind it did not reduce drift: the glossary's *Avoid* lists were followed by more uses of the names they retire. A checked rule held: the docstring-mood check has kept zero violations while the code grew. Whether written vocabulary also improves a coding agent's work is unmeasured; the published study of repository context files found no general gain in task success and a cost increase above 20%.

## Decision

**`CONTEXT.md` MUST be the project's one vocabulary document, organized as an ontology: concepts grouped in modules, each concept with one name, a namespaced identifier and a fixed set of labeled relation lines.** The document records each vocabulary decision once and is the specification later checks encode. Pydantic MUST stay the source of truth for data shapes.

1. **Modules.** The rendered part of `CONTEXT.md` has one section per module, in this order: `core` (concepts every module uses), `model` (the reference model), `composition`, `customization`, `provisioning` and `trust`. A concept moves to `core` only when a second module uses it.

1. **Entries.** Each entry opens with its `<a id="term-…">` anchor, its term in bold and its identifier, `module:Name`, then one or two sentences of definition, then these lines in this order, each left out when it does not apply:

   | Label                       | Holds                                                                     | Example                                            |
   | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
   | **Kind of**                 | The concept this one is a kind of                                         | `model:Workflow`, for the golden path              |
   | **Part of**                 | The concept this one is a part of                                         | `model:DevelopmentEnvironment`, for the toolchain  |
   | **Related**                 | Other concepts it works with                                              | `core:Template`, `composition:ScopedView`          |
   | **Not to be confused with** | A concept with a similar name and a different meaning, and the difference | `provisioning:EnvironmentProfile`, for Profile     |
   | **Stored in**               | The files that store the concept                                          | `profile.toml`                                     |
   | **Defined in**              | The source files that define or enforce it                                | `src/boilerplate/settings/profile.py`              |
   | **See**                     | The design section that owns its mechanics                                | design 04 §Scoped view                             |
   | **Avoid**                   | Retired names, as phrases                                                 | `org profile`, `config profile`                    |
   | **Carve-out**               | An allowed use of an avoided phrase                                       | "template skeleton" names `init-template`'s output |
   | **Matches**                 | An equivalent term in another vocabulary, its source, and exact or close  | paved road (Netflix, exact)                        |

1. **One concept, one name, one entry.** A term MUST be unique across all modules, compared without case, and MUST NOT appear in another entry's **Avoid** line. Two concepts that share a word each get their own term and entry, and each one's **Not to be confused with** line MUST name the other.

1. **A file is not a concept.** A file appears on the **Stored in** line of the concept it stores. A file gets its own entry only when its format is a concept in its own right.

1. **Data shapes stay in code.** An entry's **Defined in** line points at the Pydantic model or module that defines it; the entry does not restate the model's fields.

1. **Relations across modules.** The section "Rules across modules" holds only statements that span modules and that no labeled line states, such as the customization ladder Profile < Layer < Task.

1. **Drift is found by a sweep.** A read-only sweep compares the docs, the README and user-facing strings against `CONTEXT.md` and lists every synonym, conflicting copy and undefined term; the fixes land as ordinary pull requests. The sweep of 2026-10-18 found 161 findings, the baseline each later sweep's count is compared with.

1. **Automation follows evidence.** When a sweep finds drift of a kind an earlier sweep already fixed, the vocabulary moves to the form in [When the vocabulary is automated](#when-the-vocabulary-is-automated).

### Maintaining the vocabulary

- **Add a concept:** add an entry in its module with every label that applies, and link the pages that introduce the term to its anchor.
- **Rename a concept:** change the term and its anchor, keep the old anchor beside the new one so inbound links still resolve, move the old name into **Avoid**, and fix the prose the next sweep reports.
- **Split a word that means two things:** give each meaning its own term in its own module and point each one's **Not to be confused with** at the other.
- **Change behavior:** update the entry's definition and its **Defined in** line in the same pull request as the code.
- **Record a mistake:** when a contributor or an agent confuses two concepts, add or sharpen the **Not to be confused with** line on both.

### When the vocabulary is automated

The labeled lines of decision 2 are built to convert mechanically into this form, which is designed and not adopted:

- One concept file per concept, Markdown with YAML frontmatter, whose fields are the labels of decision 2.
- `CONTEXT.md` generated from the concept files, with a test that fails when the two differ.
- A pytest module that validates the frontmatter with a Pydantic model and fails on a duplicate id or term, a relation to a missing id, a cycle in **Kind of** or **Part of**, and a **Defined in** path, or a **Stored in** path under `src/` or `docs/`, that does not exist. A **Stored in** line may also name a file that lives in a generated project or the user's data directory, such as `profile.toml`, and the check skips those.
- Each domain model declaring its concept's identifier in `model_config["json_schema_extra"]["x-concept"]`, with a test that every declared identifier has an entry.
- A Vale vocabulary generated from the **Avoid** lines for the prose check, so the retired names have one source and an established tool applies them, with severities: error for a name that collides with another concept's term, warning for a softer preference.

## Options considered

- **One ontology in `CONTEXT.md`, found by sweeps (chosen).** One document is the only copy of each definition, the engineering skills keep reading the file they already read, the site keeps rendering it, and the labels give structure without new tooling.
- **One concept file per concept now** — deferred to automation. Without a generator, the concept files and `CONTEXT.md` hold two copies of every term and summary with nothing to keep them equal.
- **A SKOS concept scheme in Turtle as the source** — rejected as the source and kept as a possible export. SKOS fits the content: it models concepts as individuals rather than classes, and its hidden label matches **Avoid**. As the source it puts definitions in string literals that people and skills edit by hand and needs rdflib, pySHACL and a generator to produce the Markdown everyone reads, and SHACL Core cannot check **Kind of** for cycles without SHACL-SPARQL.
- **TBX (ISO 30042) as the source** — rejected as the source and kept as a possible export. TBX is the published standard closest to this entry model, a concept entry holding terms with preferred, admitted and deprecated status, and it is XML built for translation and exchange between termbases.
- **LinkML as the source** — rejected. LinkML describes data shapes, and many of Boilerplate's concepts (golden path, toolchain, curation) are not data shapes. Generating the domain models from LinkML makes two sources of the same shapes during the migration, and the models' hand-written validators would move into generator templates. Revisit if a data schema has to serve other languages as an equal, if RDF interoperability becomes a product feature, or if people who do not write Python need to own the model.
- **OWL** — rejected. OWL is open-world and makes no unique-name assumption, so a missing required value is not an error, and nothing in Boilerplate needs inference.
- **`CONTEXT.md` as it was** — rejected. Its *Avoid* lists retired names that prose then used more often, and relations it states only in sentences show no whole.

## Consequences

- The old Relationships list becomes "Rules across modules"; its other statements move onto labeled lines.
- Entries that name only a file fold into the concept they store, and their anchors stay beside the absorbing entry.
- `docs/agents/domain.md` tells the engineering skills that entries follow these labels. The skills themselves are the maintainer's plugins, outside this repository, and change there.
- Drift between sweeps is expected: nothing fails a build when prose uses a retired name.

## Open questions

1. **Placements.** Some concepts fit two modules, such as Guardrails in `model` or `trust`, and slot in `model` or as a term of the tool landscape. The maintainer confirms each placement the restructuring proposes.
1. **An admitted tier.** Terminology standards allow a tolerated synonym between the preferred term and a deprecated one. Whether **Avoid** needs that middle tier, for an abbreviation for example, is open.
1. **The enforcement area.** The **substrate** entry says "area" where PROD-001 says "layer". Whether "area" needs its own term, and what to do about the `enforcement_layers` key in PROD-001, which still carries the word, is open.

## Verification (2026-10-18)

I checked each external claim against its primary source on 2026-10-18. The repository facts in Context come from the files they name.

- **SKOS models concepts as individuals.** "the 'concepts' of a thesaurus or classification scheme are modeled as individuals in the SKOS data model … never as class or property axioms" ([SKOS Reference §1.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-reference/)). skos:hiddenLabel is "A lexical label for a resource that should be hidden when generating visual displays of the resource, but should still be accessible to free text search operations" ([SKOS core RDF](https://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core.rdf)).
- **SHACL Core has no cycle check.** `sh:hasValue` compares value nodes with a fixed RDF term and not with the focus node, and SHACL-SPARQL adds SELECT-based constraints ([SHACL §4.8.2, §5](https://www.w3.org/TR/shacl/)). I infer the absence of a cycle constraint from the specification; no sentence in it states one.
- **OWL makes no unique-name assumption.** "OWL does not make the assumption that different names are names for different individuals" ([OWL 2 Primer](https://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-primer/)).
- **LinkML is closed-world and writes pattern validators only by itself.** "OWL is open-world, whereas LinkML is closed-world" ([LinkML OWL generator](https://linkml.io/linkml/generators/owl.html)); "Currently the only kind of slot-level validators that are created are for those slots that have a pattern property" ([LinkML Pydantic generator](https://linkml.io/linkml/generators/pydantic.html)).
- **Terminology standards separate preferred, admitted and deprecated terms.** ANSI/NISO Z39.19 links a non-preferred synonym to its preferred term (USE/UF) and separates whole-part from genus-species hierarchy (BT/NT); ISO 12620 lists preferred, admitted and deprecated term status. I read both through published summaries, not the standards' texts.
- **Vale reads vocabularies independently of its styles.** Vale feeds a vocabulary's rejected terms into `Vale.Avoid` ([Vale vocabularies](https://docs.vale.sh/keys/vocabularies)), and GitLab fails its docs CI on error-level Vale rules ([GitLab docs testing](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/documentation/testing/vale/)).
- **Context files have no measured general benefit.** Gloaguen et al. report that context files "do not generally improve task success rates" and raise inference cost by more than 20% ([arXiv 2602.11988](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988)). The study tested overviews and tooling instructions, not glossaries.
- **This repository's history.** I measured rules at dated snapshots of the archive repository (2026-05-11 to 2026-09-04) and of `develop` (from 2026-09-04), and reran at least one number per rule.
  - Of 556 commits authored while the commit-message rules existed only in prose, 22 had a subject over 72 characters; of 667 authored once `scripts/commit_lint.py` existed, none did. A model new to the repository wrote most of the later commits, so the check is not the only cause.
  - The docstring-mood rule changed twice in prose, and neither change moved existing code; the count fell to zero when a sweep rewrote the code and the D401 check turned on, and it stayed at zero as public functions grew from 102 to 270.
  - After the *Avoid* lists were written, "template variable" rose from 14 to 16 uses in the docs and "overlay" for a layer from 0 to 8.
  - The limits: one project, no control group, gates record only what landed, and maintainer corrections made in conversation leave no trace in git.

# ADR-017: Build backend — `uv_build` by default, `hatchling` by choice

**Status**: Accepted

> **Scope note.** This ADR fixes which build backends the `project` template offers, which one it renders by default, how the `uv_build` version bound stays current, and how an existing project keeps its backend through `copier update`. For what exists today, see [status.md](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/status/index.md).

## Context

The `project` template renders a pure-Python package with a static version and one `src/<package_name>` directory, and its toolchain is built on uv ([dev-environment landscape](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/dev-environment-landscape/#how-boilerplate-maps-onto-the-landscape)). The `streamlit` template extends `project`, so it renders the same `[build-system]` table. The build backend is the one slot of that toolchain that the mapping table leaves unfilled, and Boilerplate's rule for slots is one opinionated pick each, with a named override.

Projects rendered before this decision declare `hatchling` with no version bound. Three facts bear on the pick:

- **uv ships its own backend.** `uv_build` is the backend that plain `uv init` declares since uv 0.12.0, and uv's documentation calls it "a great choice for most Python projects" ([uv build backend](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/build-backend/)). It builds pure Python only.
- **uv's own docs name the escape hatch.** The documentation advises that "when build scripts or a more flexible project layout are required, consider using the hatchling build backend instead" ([uv build backend](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/build-backend/)). `hatchling` runs build hooks and plugins, reads the version from git tags through `hatch-vcs`, and selects files with its own configuration.
- **A backend cap needs upkeep.** uv bumps its minor version for breaking changes and its patch version for everything else ([uv versioning policy](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/policies/versioning/)), and its documentation tells `uv_build` users to cap the requirement at the next minor. uv released 0.12.0 on 2026-07-28 and 0.13.0 on 2026-10-09, so a cap of that kind needs a bump every few months.

A render that picks a backend also decides what happens when `copier update` meets a project rendered earlier. A new question with a default is applied silently by `copier update --defaults`, so adding the question without a migration moves every existing `hatchling` project to `uv_build`. That move drops any `[tool.hatch]` configuration and any `dynamic = ["version"]` entry the project relies on, and narrows the sdist from every file git does not ignore to the package and its metadata. [Versioning § What qualifies as breaking](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/governance/versioning/#what-qualifies-as-breaking) classes "changing the default value of an option incompatibly" as breaking.

## Decision

**The `project` template MUST ask a `build_backend` question with two choices, `uv_build` (the default) and `hatchling`, and MUST render the `[build-system]` table, plus the `[tool.hatch]` table for `hatchling`, from that answer.** The `streamlit` template inherits the question from `project` and does not redeclare it.

1. **The question.** `build_backend` is a `str` question with `choices`, placed before `package_index_url` in the `project` template's `copier.yml`. Its choices are the two backend names, with no description on either; the project template guide says when to pick each.
1. **The `uv_build` render.** The template renders `requires = ["uv_build>=0.13,<0.14"]` and `build-backend = "uv_build"`, with no `[tool.hatch]` table. `uv_build` finds `src/<package_name>` without configuration.
1. **The `hatchling` render.** The template renders `requires = ["hatchling>=1.27"]`, `build-backend = "hatchling.build"` and the `[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]` table with `packages = ["src/<package_name>"]`. Hatchling 1.27.0 is the first release that writes the PEP 639 license fields (`License-Expression`, `License-File`) by default; 1.26.x writes the old `License:` field. The requirement has no cap, the same as `hatch new` writes it.
1. **The bound is a minor range.** The `uv_build` requirement takes the current uv minor as its floor (`>=0.13`, not `>=0.13.3`), so every uv 0.13.x runs its bundled copy of the backend and fetches nothing from a package index. A private `package_index_url` therefore mirrors no build backend for a project inside the range.
1. **The bound moves with the Docker tag.** The `streamlit` template's Dockerfile installs uv from the image tag `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:<minor>`. For every uv minor, the `uv_build` range and that tag move together in one change, and a test renders `streamlit` and asserts that the range's minor equals the tag's minor. An image older than the range's floor fetches `uv-build` from the package index and fails offline with a cold cache, which is the reason for the pairing. The test catches drift between the two values and does not catch staleness, so the release checklist in `RELEASING.md` names the uv minor, and uv's own warning (point 6) tells a user that a generated project's cap is stale.
1. **uv's behavior outside the range.** uv uses its bundled backend only when `requires` is a single `uv_build` entry whose range contains uv's version. A uv newer than the cap (0.13.3 against `<0.13`) builds with its bundled copy and warns on every `uv sync` and `uv build`. A uv older than the floor fetches `uv-build` from the index, as the documentation describes. The documentation's statement that an out-of-range uv "uses a compatible version of the `uv_build` package" describes only the second case.
1. **A `before` migration keeps existing projects on `hatchling`.** The `project` template's `copier.yml` declares its first `_migrations` entry with `when: "{{ _stage == 'before' }}"` and no `version` gate: bundled layers share the repository's tag stream, so a gate at the version that introduces the question would skip a project rendered at the tag just before it, and the key check below makes the entry a no-op once the answer exists. The migration runs the update's Python (`{{ _copier_python }}`) to append `build_backend: hatchling` to the layer's answers file (`.copier-answers.project.yml`, passed to the script as `{{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}`) when that file exists and holds no `build_backend` key. `copier update --defaults` then keeps a project rendered before the question existed on `hatchling`, and an explicit `--data build_backend=hatchling` keeps it as well. A project that has a `build_backend` answer is untouched.
1. **Switching is a re-answer.** A project that changes backend after generation re-answers the question with `copier update --data build_backend=<choice>`, which re-renders the `[build-system]` table and the `[tool.hatch]` table together.

### When to choose which backend

The table covers the nine backends a Python project most often meets; the two the template offers come first. It leaves out `whey`, which had four sdists in the Quansight Labs sample, `py-build-cmake`, which has about 31 thousand downloads a month, and `enscons`, which has about 10 thousand downloads a month and little activity. A backend outside the first two is a hand edit of `[build-system]` in the generated project, and the template scaffolds no `Cargo.toml` or `CMakeLists.txt` for the compiled rows.

| Backend                  | Choose it when                                                                                | Avoid it when                                                                                                                  | Notes: PEP 639, editable installs, version bounds                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **`uv_build`** (default) | Pure Python; static version; one `src/<package>`; uv toolchain                                | Version from git tags; build hooks; generated files that git ignores inside the package; several top-level packages            | PEP 639 output. PEP 660 editable hook. Bound `>=0.13,<0.14`; uv's documentation caps at the next minor                                                                          |
| **`hatchling`**          | Build hooks; version from git (`hatch-vcs`); custom file selection; plugins                   | A build that must fetch no build requirement (`uv_build` runs from uv's bundled copy); native extensions without a custom hook | PEP 639 output by default from 1.27.0 (1.26.x writes the old `License:` field). Editable installs through a `.pth` file. Floor `>=1.27`, no cap                                 |
| **`setuptools`**         | Existing `setup.py` or `cmdclass`; small C extension through `ext_modules`; `setuptools-rust` | New pure-Python project; non-`.py` data without `package-data` (the wheel silently omits it)                                   | PEP 639 from 77.0.1, the first release on PyPI (77.0.0 was never published); the PyPA tutorial uses `>=77.0.3`. Editable installs from 64.0.0; a binary extension is a snapshot |
| **`flit-core`**          | Tiny module; `__version__` as the version; nothing else                                       | Hooks; git versioning; generated files                                                                                         | PEP 639 from 3.11. Flit's documentation: `>=3.11,<5`; the PyPA tutorial tab: `>=3.12.0,<5`                                                                                      |
| **`pdm-backend`**        | The team runs PDM; built-in SCM version                                                       | A uv-run project, where PDM's workflow owns the lock                                                                           | PEP 639 from 2.4.0. Editable installs through `path` or `editables`. PyPA tutorial: `>=2.4.0`                                                                                   |
| **`poetry-core`**        | The team runs Poetry; no extension modules                                                    | A uv-run project; extension modules (Poetry calls its build scripts "still considered unstable")                               | `[project]` table from 2.0.0; PEP 639 from 2.2.0. Poetry's documentation: `>=2.0.0,<3.0.0`                                                                                      |
| **`maturin`**            | Rust through PyO3, cffi or uniffi                                                             | Code with no Rust                                                                                                              | PEP 639 in full from 1.9.0 and the `License-Expression` fix in 1.9.2. A Rust edit needs a rebuild. `uv init` scaffolds it and writes `cache-keys`                               |
| **`scikit-build-core`**  | C, C++, Fortran or Cython with CMake, pybind11 or nanobind                                    | A codebase with no CMake                                                                                                       | PEP 639 from 0.11.0. Editable redirect; rebuild-on-import is experimental. `uv init --build-backend scikit` scaffolds it                                                        |
| **`meson-python`**       | A Meson codebase; the numerics stack (numpy and scipy build with it)                          | A project that wants `uv init` scaffolding or automatic `cache-keys`                                                           | PEP 639 from 0.18.0. Editable rebuild-on-import needs `--no-build-isolation`. `uv init` rejects it                                                                              |

## Options considered

- **`uv_build` default, `hatchling` by choice (chosen).** The default covers the template's shape (pure Python, static version, one `src/<package_name>`) and is the backend uv itself scaffolds. `hatchling` is the one other backend that does a job `uv_build` does not for this template: hooks, plugins, and a version from git. Each of the two has a stated trigger in the question's help strings.
- **`hatchling` as the default (the runner-up).** The PyPA packaging tutorial states "this tutorial uses Hatchling by default" ([packaging projects](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/tutorials/packaging-projects/)), and the Scientific Python Development Guide says "If you don't have an existing preference, hatchling is an excellent choice" ([packaging simple](https://github.com/scientific-python/cookie/blob/main/docs/guides/packaging_simple.md)). `hatchling` needs no cap upkeep. PyPI recorded about 320 million `hatchling` downloads and about 15 million `uv-build` downloads in the month before 2026-10-19 ([pypistats](https://pypistats.org/api/packages/hatchling/recent)); pip build isolation and CI inflate both counts, so they are not adoption shares. Rejected: the template's toolchain is uv, uv recommends `uv_build` for this project shape, and the cap has cost only bumps so far, because each uv release note states "no breaking changes to the configuration of the uv build backend" ([uv changelogs](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/tree/main/changelogs)). What would change the call: uv dropping or loosening its cap advice, or a usage census that shows `uv_build` adoption stalling.
- **A wider menu (setuptools, flit-core, pdm-backend, poetry-core and the compiled backends).** Rejected, because a menu is not a pick and each extra choice has to do a job neither default nor override does for this template.
  - `setuptools` adds extension and legacy-`setup.py` use, which the template does not scaffold, and its wheel omits non-`.py` data files without a `package-data` entry.
  - `flit-core` does less than `uv_build` for this shape.
  - `pdm-backend` and `poetry-core` belong to the PDM and Poetry workflows, whose tools own the lock; that contradicts the uv pick in the landscape mapping table.
  - The compiled backends need source scaffolding (`Cargo.toml`, `CMakeLists.txt`), `cache-keys`, and a compiler stage in the `streamlit` Dockerfile.
- **Derive the `uv_build` bound from the running uv at render time.** Rejected. It matches what `uv init` does, and the `project` template has precedent: `_extensions/context.py` derives the Python version from the running interpreter. The render would then depend on the machine that runs it, and the bound would split from the static Docker image tag that point 5 pairs it with.
- **Choose the default by operation, so that `copier update` defaults to `hatchling` and `copy` defaults to `uv_build`.** Rejected, because Copier exposes `_copier_operation` only in `exclude` and `_tasks`, not in a question's `default` ([Copier: creating a template](https://copier.readthedocs.io/en/stable/creating/)). The before-stage migration of point 7 is the mechanism Copier documents for changing answers across versions.

## Consequences

- **The cap needs upkeep.** The `uv_build` range and the `streamlit` Dockerfile tag move for every uv minor (point 5). Dependabot's `uv` and `github-actions` ecosystems update only this repository's own files, so no updater reaches a `.jinja` file, and the release checklist is the reminder.
- **`uv_build` ships git-ignored files.** It does not read `.gitignore`: a git-ignored file inside the package directory reaches both the wheel and the sdist. `hatchling` honors `.gitignore`. Nothing the template renders today sits in that position. A project that generates files into its package tree sets `source-exclude` and `wheel-exclude` under `[tool.uv.build-backend]`, or chooses `hatchling`.
- **`uv_build` builds from static metadata.** A non-empty `dynamic` list fails the build with "Dynamic metadata is not supported". A project that wants a version from git tags chooses `hatchling` and `hatch-vcs`.
- **The migration is one more reason `copier update` needs `--trust`, not a new requirement.** The `project` layer already declares `_jinja_extensions`, including the file-path `_extensions/context.py`, and `_tasks`, so Copier's unsafe check refuses an update of it without `--trust`. [Versioning](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/templates-hub/versioning/index.md) also lists running `copier update` across any declared migration as a step that refuses to start without `--trust`. Layers that Boilerplate bundles are copy-only ([ADR-015](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-015-idiomatic-artifacts/index.md)), so only a project rendered from a git-backed `project` layer meets the migration.
- **The migration is the reason the change is not breaking.** With it, adding `build_backend` is "adding a new template variable (with a sensible default)" under [Versioning](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/governance/versioning/#what-qualifies-as-breaking); without it, the change is the incompatible default change the Context describes. The migration reads and writes the answers file, which is Copier's file layout and not a Copier API, so the template version that ships it MUST pass a test that updates a `hatchling` project and asserts that its backend is unchanged.
- **Boilerplate's own `pyproject.toml` follows the same default.** The repository is a pure-Python package with a static version and one `src/boilerplate`, the shape for which `uv_build` is the pick.

## Verification (2026-10-20)

The sources below were read on 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20, and the trials ran in scratch projects under uv 0.13.3 and Copier 9.18.1. Repository facts in the Context come from the files they name.

- **uv.** Documentation: "a great choice for most Python projects", pure Python only, hatchling for build scripts, and the bound `>=0.13.3,<0.14` as the example ([build backend](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/build-backend/)). `uv init` declares `uv_build` for plain apps since 0.12.0 ([changelog 0.12.x](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/changelogs/0.12.x.md)); uv 0.13.3 writes `uv_build>=0.13.3,<0.14.0` into a new project. The minor-for-breaking policy is in [versioning](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/policies/versioning/). `uv_build` rejects a non-empty `dynamic` list in `crates/uv-build-backend/src/metadata.rs` ([source](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/crates/uv-build-backend/src/metadata.rs)), and a trial with uv 0.13.3 reproduced the message. The out-of-range behavior in point 6 comes from uv 0.13.3 against `<0.13` (bundled copy, warning) and uv 0.12.15 against a floor above its version (index fetch).
- **File selection.** In a trial with a git-ignored file inside the package and one in a generated subdirectory, `uv_build` shipped both and `hatchling` shipped neither.
- **hatchling.** 1.27.0 is the first release that writes `License-Expression`; 1.26.3 writes Metadata 2.3 with the old `License:` field and no `License-Expression` ([hatchling history](https://hatch.pypa.io/latest/history/hatchling/); wheel inspected for both). The PyPA tutorial's `hatchling >= 1.26` is therefore short of PEP 639 output by default.
- **PyPA tutorial tabs.** `hatchling >= 1.26`, `setuptools >= 77.0.3`, `flit_core >=3.12.0,<5`, `pdm-backend >= 2.4.0` ([build-backend-tabs.rst](https://github.com/pypa/packaging.python.org/blob/main/source/shared/build-backend-tabs.rst)).
- **setuptools.** PEP 639 in the 77.0.0 notes, and PyPI lists 77.0.1 and 77.0.3 but not 77.0.0; PEP 660 in 64.0.0 ([NEWS](https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/blob/main/NEWS.rst), [PyPI JSON](https://pypi.org/pypi/setuptools/json)). A trial wheel omitted `.txt` and dotfile data that no `package-data` entry listed.
- **flit-core.** `flit_core >=3.11,<5` and PEP 639 from 3.11 ([pyproject.toml docs](https://flit.pypa.io/en/stable/pyproject_toml.html)).
- **pdm-backend.** Version 2.4.0 writes `License-Expression` and `License-File`; 2.4.5 and 2.5.0 write them as well (wheels inspected). The 2.4.6 changelog entry "Add license file metadata" edits pdm-backend's own `pyproject.toml` and does not change the built metadata. The PDM documentation is at [backend.pdm-project.org](https://backend.pdm-project.org/).
- **poetry-core.** `[project]` support in 2.0.0, PEP 639 in 2.2.0, `>=2.0.0,<3.0.0` in the docs, and build scripts "still considered unstable" ([CHANGELOG](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry-core/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md), [extension modules](https://python-poetry.org/docs/building-extension-modules/)).
- **Compiled backends.** maturin: PEP 639 in 1.9.0 and the `License-Expression` fix in 1.9.2 ([Changelog](https://github.com/PyO3/maturin/blob/main/Changelog.md)). scikit-build-core: PEP 639 in 0.11.0 ([changelog](https://github.com/scikit-build/scikit-build-core/blob/main/docs/about/changelog.md)). meson-python: PEP 639 in 0.18.0 ([CHANGELOG](https://github.com/mesonbuild/meson-python/blob/main/CHANGELOG.rst)). `uv init` offers maturin and scikit-build-core and rejects meson-python ([uv init](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/init/)). numpy and scipy build with meson-python, which their `pyproject.toml` files declare.
- **Bounds in each backend's own scaffold.** `hatch new` writes an unbounded `hatchling`; `flit init` writes `flit_core >=3.11,<5`; `poetry new` writes a range from the installed `poetry-core`.
- **Render trial.** A scratch copy of the `project` template was rendered with each choice. Each render passed validate-pyproject and ran `uv lock`, `uv sync`, pytest and `uv build` under uv 0.13.3. The `hatchling` render differs from the output of earlier template versions on the `requires` line only.
- **Update trial.** On a toy template with a `build_backend` question added after the project's first render, `copier update --defaults` moved a `hatchling` project to `uv_build`; with the before-stage migration it stayed on `hatchling`, and `--data build_backend=hatchling` kept it as well.
- **Omitted backends.** `whey` had four sdists in the Quansight Labs sample ([PEP 517 build system popularity](https://labs.quansight.org/blog/pep-517-build-system-popularity)); `py-build-cmake` and `enscons` download figures come from pypistats, and their projects are [py-build-cmake](https://github.com/tttapa/py-build-cmake) and [enscons](https://github.com/dholth/enscons).
- **Copier.** `_copier_operation` is documented for `exclude` and `_tasks` only ([creating a template](https://copier.readthedocs.io/en/stable/creating/)).

### Limits

- The update trial used a toy template with the answers file `.copier-answers.yml`. The `project` template's own answers file, `.copier-answers.project.yml`, was not exercised, which is the reason point 7 requires an update test in the template's suite.
- No Docker image was built. The behavior of the `streamlit` image under the `uv:0.13` tag and the `>=0.13,<0.14` range follows from the uv documentation and the 0.12.15 trial.
- The editable and rebuild behavior of maturin, scikit-build-core and meson-python comes from their documentation; no compiler was available to run them.
- Whether Dependabot's `uv` ecosystem updates a `[build-system]` requirement in a generated project was not tested.
- The newest usage census (Quansight Labs, "PEP 517 build system popularity", published 2025-02-11) reports no `uv_build` count; it was read through its markdown source and its figures were not re-checked. The download counts in the options are monthly totals, and they serve for the order of magnitude only.

## Relationship to other ADRs

- [ADR-001](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-001-build-vs-adopt/index.md) — uv's own backend and `hatchling` are adopted tools; Boilerplate adds only the choice between them.
- [ADR-003](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-003-permissive-execution/index.md) and [ADR-007](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-007-update-model/index.md) — the `before` migration of point 7 is a first-party migration, the kind that ADR-007 makes the mechanism for structural change and that ADR-003 puts on the task and extension trust surface.
- [ADR-015](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-015-idiomatic-artifacts/index.md) — the migration edits the per-layer answers file `.copier-answers.project.yml`, which that ADR makes the distribution contract, and Copier's own `_migrations` mechanism runs it.

# The Development Environment Landscape

The reference taxonomy of what a Python development environment comprises. Boilerplate's design vocabulary calls each recurring role in this taxonomy a [slot](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-slot). This document catalogues the landscape; the [§How Boilerplate maps onto the landscape](#how-boilerplate-maps-onto-the-landscape) section records which slots Boilerplate opines on.

> **Provenance.** Transcribed from the project author's *Python Development Environment* mind map, committed alongside this document as the [XMind source](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/assets/python-development-environment.xmind). This transcription is the repo-canonical text form. Category definitions are the author's; example tools are illustrative, not exhaustive, and not endorsements.

## Definition

Tools, libraries, and configurations that enable scalable and maintainable Python application development, enhancing productivity, code quality, reliability, and maintainability.

## Taxonomy

### Environment

The context in which Python code runs, including the interpreter, libraries, and configurations. Effective environments ensure isolated and reproducible builds, reducing conflicts between dependencies. (In this taxonomy, *Environment* names the runtime context specifically — a narrower sense than the glossary's domain-level term.)

- **Python Interpreter** — software that reads and executes Python code. Examples: CPython, PyPy, IronPython, Jython, GraalPy, MicroPython, Stackless Python.
- **Environment Management** — tools for isolating project dependencies, preventing conflicts, and ensuring consistent builds. Examples: venv, conda, uv.

### Package/Dependency Management

Software that simplifies the installation, upgrading, and removal of Python libraries, ensuring projects have the correct versions of all required packages. Examples: pip, poetry, conda, pip-tools, pipenv, uv.

### Development Tools

Software and utilities that automate repetitive tasks, profile performance, and facilitate experimentation and prototyping.

- **Interactive Development Environments** — platforms combining code, visualizations, and explanatory text for experimentation and collaboration.
  - *Notebook Environments* — Jupyter Notebook, Google Colab, Deepnote.
  - *Remote Development Environments* — workspaces accessible via a network or abstracted from the primary local machine. Examples: GitHub Codespaces, Microsoft DevBox, Dev Containers.
  - *Interactive Shells* — advanced REPLs. Example: IPython.
- **Debugging Tools** — identifying and resolving code issues. Examples: pdb, ipdb, debugpy.
- **Build & Automation**
  - *Build Tools* — compile, package, and distribute projects into installable formats. Examples: setuptools, hatch, wheel.
  - *Task Runners* — automate repetitive development tasks for consistent workflows. Examples: invoke, nox.
- **Performance Profiling** — identify bottlenecks and optimize execution. Examples: cProfile, line_profiler, timeit, memory_profiler, py-spy, gprof2dot.

### Code Management Tools

Tools and utilities that streamline collaboration, improve code quality, and track changes throughout the software development lifecycle.

- **Version Control Systems** — track changes to source code over time, enabling collaboration, branching, merging, and reverting. Examples: Git, Mercurial.
- **Code Review Workflows** — processes for evaluating proposed changes (pull/merge requests) to ensure quality and share knowledge. Examples: GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab, Bitbucket.
- **Collaboration Tools** — planning, task coordination, and discussion. Examples: Azure DevOps Boards, GitHub Projects, GitLab Issues, Trello/Jira, Slack/Teams.

### IDEs & Editors

Applications providing a suite of development features — syntax highlighting, refactoring, debugging, version-control integration — to streamline coding workflows. Examples: PyCharm, Visual Studio Code, Spyder, Jupyter Notebook, Thonny.

### Code Quality Tools

Software that ensures Python code adheres to style guidelines, avoids errors, and remains maintainable.

- **Linters** — inspect code without running it to identify style issues, errors, or potential bugs. Examples: Flake8, Pylint, Ruff.
- **Code Formatters** — reformat source code to a consistent style. Examples: Black, YAPF, Ruff.
- **Type Checkers** — validate code against type annotations, catching errors early. Examples: mypy, Pyright.
- **Testing Frameworks** — create, organize, and execute automated tests.
  - *Core Frameworks* — pytest, unittest.
  - *Environment Management for tests* — tox, nox.
  - *Mocking* — unittest.mock, pytest-mock.
  - *Code Coverage* — coverage, pytest-cov.

### Deployment Tools

Technologies for packaging and deploying Python applications, automating processes and enhancing scalability.

- **Containerization** — *Containers* (Docker, Rancher Desktop) and *Container Orchestration* (Kubernetes, Rancher).
- **Serverless** — AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions.
- **CI/CD** — continuous integration and deployment platforms. Examples: GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, Jenkins, TeamCity.
- **Infrastructure as Code** — Terraform, Ansible.
- **Platform as a Service** — Heroku, Google App Engine, Azure App Service.

### Security Tools

Tools that enhance the security and integrity of Python applications.

- **Static Analysis** — Bandit, Semgrep.
- **Dependency Scanning** — Safety, Dependabot, Snyk.
- **Secrets Management** — Doppler, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault.
- **Monitoring and Observability** — New Relic, Datadog, Sentry, Prometheus, Grafana.

### Documentation Tools

Tools and standards for creating and maintaining project documentation.

- **Docstring Standards** — reStructuredText, Google style, NumPy style.
- **Documentation Generators** — Sphinx, MkDocs.

### Data and Visualization Tools

Tools for manipulating, analyzing, and visualizing data.

- **Data Analysis** — pandas, numpy.
- **Visualization** — matplotlib, seaborn, Plotly.

### Learning and Experimentation

Interactive platforms and hosted environments for learning Python, prototyping, and experimenting. Examples: Jupyter Notebook, Google Colab.

## How Boilerplate maps onto the landscape

Each first-party template fills the slots its ecosystem's [dev loop](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-dev-loop) uses — the roles a developer exercises on every pass through it — with one opinionated, preconfigured pick each, declared through the profile the template requires. The Python picks:

| Slot                                                   | Pick                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Environment Management + Package/Dependency Management | uv                                                                                                                                               |
| Linters + Code Formatters                              | Ruff                                                                                                                                             |
| Type Checkers                                          | Pyright                                                                                                                                          |
| Testing Frameworks (core, mocking, coverage)           | pytest, pytest-mock, pytest-cov                                                                                                                  |
| Build Tools                                            | uv_build, with hatchling as the override ([ADR-017](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-017-build-backend/index.md)) |
| IDEs & Editors                                         | VS Code                                                                                                                                          |
| Version Control Systems                                | Git                                                                                                                                              |

Two rules give the mapping its shape:

- **Templates declare their slots and fill them.** A template's required profile names the tool per slot, including any secondary toolchain its kind of project needs (the `streamlit` template needs Docker and Bash; on Windows, WSL2); the environment installs and verifies what the profile declares; the template pre-wires each tool's per-project configuration — Ruff's rule set, Pyright's strictness, pytest's options, the `.vscode/` workspace settings — and scaffolds adjacent slots such as CI/CD and documentation generation as [gating scaffolding](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#term-first-party-gating-scaffolding) the user opts into.
- **Slots no first-party template requires are out of scope by design.** The remaining landscape (profiling, serverless, IaC, PaaS, data tooling, …) is a scope boundary: "should Boilerplate also do X?" is answered by whether some first-party template's kind of project needs X on its golden path. Containerization enters through the `streamlit` template's required profile.

The development environment built from these picks is itself a first-class, managed surface — installation, verification, update, and drift detection across its lifecycle — per [01-overview.md §Environment lifecycle is managed](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/01-overview/#environment-lifecycle-is-managed) and the provisioning design in [§08](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/08-environment-provisioning/index.md) / [ADR-009](https://therealbillsiegler.github.io/boilerplate/0.4/design/adr-009-environment-provider-protocol/index.md).
